#9552. The Best Celebrity Red Wines, According To Our Editors

These bottles have some serious star power.

Celebrities have taken over the liquor store, with everyone from rappers to actors to athletes launching their own bottles. And the section with the most star power is definitely the wine aisle.

Whether they own their own vineyards or simply slap their names on a label, celebrities sell wines from almost every corner of the world. To see whether any of them are worth the A-list endorsements, we tasted a selection of their most popular red wines. Here are the ones that won over Delish editors.

Cameron Diaz's wine brand, Avaline, specializes in bottles made with organically farmed grapes and minimal additives. Avaline's red blend is made in France with Rhône varietals like Grenache and Syrah.

Our editors appreciated its light- to medium-bodied flavor and bone-dry finish. Notes of red fruit and light spice add just enough depth to keep each sip interesting. And at $24 per bottle, this is a solid table wine that tastes much more expensive than it is.

Reality TV legend Lisa Vanderpump is no stranger to the food and beverage business. In addition to operating six restaurants, she’s also the mind behind her eponymous wine brand. And LVP’s Sonoma County Cabernet Sauvignon is as elegant and sophisticated as she is.

While other Cabernets can be bold and intense, this wine's beauty lies in its subtlety. One editor described it as a “summer Cab” because of its soft, delicate fruit profile. The flavor is complex without feeling too rich or heavy, making it an ideal red for dinner. And at $26 a bottle, it’s a good deal, too.

Famed film director Francis Ford Coppola isn’t just known for his Oscar-winning movies—he’s also a prolific winemaker. He sold his namesake winery to Delicato Family Wines in 2021, but the lineup is still just as strong as it was under his leadership.

We enjoyed all of Coppola’s reds, but the Archimedes Cabernet Sauvignon was a clear standout. Made with California-grown grapes and aged for 20 months in French and American oak barrels, this wine delivers what our editors described as the quintessential Cab, with a full-bodied, smooth flavor and notes of dark fruit and tobacco.

Depending on the vintage and retailer, prices can start around $70 and climb past $100. But if you want to impress both the film buffs and wine snobs in your life, it’s worth the splurge.

#9548. Vegan Pumpkin Pie

PSA: This vegan pumpkin pie is so good, it might rival the classic. It’s just as easy as any other pumpkin pie recipe, if not easier. Bonus points: the nutty, pecan-based crust is naturally gluten-free! Using coconut oil in the crust and coconut milk in the filling, I was able to replicate the richness of pumpkin pie without sacrificing any flavor. This vegan treat will satisfy those pumpkin pie cravings, but with a unique nutty crust that amplifies all the fall flavors.

What People Are Saying:“This is my family's FAVORITE vegan pumpkin pie - we make it every year…” - GoldPaw

The best part about this pie is that you don’t need to chill the pie dough at all. Preheat your oven to 375° and grease your pie plate.

Then, use a food processor to pulse the pecans, oats, sugar, and salt until they’re fine crumbs. Stream in the coconut oil and then pulse until the dough forms. You’re done! The easiest pie dough you’ll ever make.

Press the dough into your greased pie plate in an even layer– make sure you press the dough up the sides of the pan as well. Place parchment over the dough and fill with dried beans, rice, or pie weights. Bake for 10 minutes and then remove the parchment and bake for another 10 minutes.

To make the filling, whisk all of the filling ingredients together in a large bowl. Pour it into the par-baked crust, smoothing the top.

Bake the pie in the oven for 50 to 55 minutes. If the crust starts to get too dark, cover the whole pie with foil. You’ll know the pie is done when it looks set and dry on top but is still slightly jiggly in the center. Let cool in the refrigerator before serving with some whipped topping alongside.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

Keep your pie in the fridge for up to 4 days, loosely covered with foil. Keep the whipped cream separate and dollop onto each pie slice as you serve. If the whipped cream loses structure, keep it cold and re-whip with a handheld mixer as needed.

#9542. Apple Galette

Honestly, we can’t think of anything better than a galette. They've got all the delicious elements of pie—flaky, buttery crust and tender baked fruit—but none of the fussy technique. With galettes, you don’t have to worry about any crimping, latticework, or blind baking. Sometimes, it's okay to take the easy road. This classic apple galette is one of our favorite examples. Warm, comforting, and bursting with sweet, spiced flavor, it’s everything you love about apple pie with a fraction of the effort.

What People Are Saying:“I've already made this twice. Really really nice recipe. So fast and simple, not too sweet and not at all goopy. This will be my go-to filling for apple galettes from now on.” - PurpleRing

First, combine the apples, brown sugar, lemon juice, cinnamon, and salt in a large bowl. Then, preheat the oven to 400° and prepare a baking sheet by lining it with parchment paper. Coat a clean surface with a dusting of flour, then roll the chilled pie dough into a 12” circle that is about ⅛” thick. Transfer the dough to the baking sheet.

Arrange the apple slices on top of the dough in alternating rows, leaving about a 1 ½” border around the edge. Then, fold the dough edge nearest to you toward the center and rotate the baking sheet, repeating this step until all 4 edges of the dough are folded in toward the fruit.

Brush the egg wash over the crust and sprinkle demerara sugar over the top. Then place the galette into the oven to bake for 40 to 45 minutes until the crust is golden brown and the fruit is fragrant and tender. Remove the galette from the oven and transfer it to a cooling rack to cool completely before slicing and serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

A galette is essentially an open-faced pie. Thinly sliced apples are tossed in cinnamon and sugar and layered on top of a single sheet of pie crust. The crust is folded over the apples in a rough circle and baked until the crust is flaky. Apple pie has a top and bottom crust and is usually formed in a pie dish. The extra crust and overall shape are the only real differences, and for the apple obsessed, galettes provide the perfect ratio of crust to filling.

Anything you'd serve with an apple pie would work here as well. That means your favorite ice cream, frozen yogurt, caramel sauce, or candied nuts would be great galette sidekicks.

Any leftover galette can be stored for up to 4 days in the refrigerator.

#9539. COVID-19 and Moral Injury: a Mental Health Pandemic for Frontline Health Care Workers

More than 2 years ago, the alarm and first warnings of a global pandemic sounded. Now with over 830,000 deaths caused by COVID-19 in the US, there looms on the horizon a second underlying curve with equally serious long-term consequences: a mental health pandemic.

The mental health fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic demands recognition, intervention, and mitigation strategies. Among the many at-risk populations are frontline health care workers who have been at the epicenter of the global pandemic, working long shifts with at times a tenuous safety net and limited support, and caring for COVID-19 patients with limited resources, mixed messaging, and uncertainty with regards to an end to the crisis. The psychological effects in some health care providers are akin to the moral trauma or moral injury that is recognized in combat veterans with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Mental health professionals and other health care providers caring for frontline health care workers who present with insomnia, depression, anxiety, panic attacks, PTSD, and suicidal thoughts should recognize and validate their experiences and moral injury. Intervention strategies including health promotion, resilience training, and ongoing multilevel support will play an important role in flattening the moral injury curve.

As a rule, the frontline health care workforce is considered capable, competent, resilient, professional, and persevering in the face of adversity. However, COVID-19 presented as an unprecedented crisis unlike any other unforeseen disaster, eliciting fear, uncertainty, and anxiety, coupled with grief and loss, both personally and professionally.1 As noted by Warren D. Taylor, MD, MHSc, and Jennifer Urbano Blackford, PhD1:

The pandemic created anxiety and fear in health care providers, from physicians and nurses to allied health professionals and first-line responders. We fear for the safety of our families and patients. We grieve for those who have died. We feel guilt for not being able to save all our patients, for getting sick ourselves, and for abandoning our families. Many adopted the phrase, “we will get through this together but none of us will survive unscathed.”

At the outset, the shortage of equipment and resources, changing practice guidelines, and unpredictability of the workload rendered health care workers with a sense of powerlessness and loss of control of the conditions under which they were able to deliver care. The emotional distress and social isolation from family and friends exacted an immeasurable toll on the physical health and emotional well-being of the workforce, setting the stage for the inevitable moral injury.2

Moral injury is a term that has been applied to veterans of combat. Moral injury or moral distress as experienced by frontline health care providers occurs when health care providers are forced to make decisions that transgress their professional commitment to patient comfort and care, and forcibly shift their moral compass. They are not able to meet the physical, emotional, and end-of-life needs of patients.3

Watson et al noted that moral injury in health care workers “can occur when someone engages in, fails to prevent, or witnesses acts that conflict with their values or beliefs.”4 Moral injuries may result from the following, according to Watson et al4:

The consequences of such experiences may include feelings of rage, guilt, shame, and anger and moral injury is the “lasting psychological, spiritual, behavioral or social impact that may result from these experiences.”4 The number of acutely ill COVID-19 patients and high death rate coupled with lack of resources and at times rationing of limited resources such as personal protective equipment (PPE) and ventilators added to the dilemma that frontline health care workers faced.

In a study of 448 Jordanian nurses during the COVID-19 pandemic, the majority of nurses (64%) reported experiencing acute stress disorder (ASD) and 41% reported significant psychological distress, with a predilection for younger nurses compared to older nurses.5 However, coping self-efficacy was a protective factor with the potential to mitigate the severity of psychological distress.5 An online survey of nonhealth care providers (N=976) found that individuals with previous trauma were at highest risk for increased symptoms of anxiety, depression, and PTSD related to COVID-19 compared with individuals with no previous history of trauma.6

The long-term mental health consequences of moral injury for frontline health care workers have important implications for workforce survivability and durability; however, research on this topic is lacking. In one of the few published studies on moral injury among health care providers, investigators looked at the thematic content of experiences reported by nurses following incidents meeting the contextual definition of moral injury (ie, events with unintended consequences, potentially causing patient harm or putting patients at risk for serious injury). The investigators found nurses reported experiencing “guilt, shame, spiritual–existential crisis, and loss of trust.”7

COVID-19 has presented difficult and untenable working conditions beyond the scope of the challenges frontline health care workers are prepared for professionally. Frontline health care workers have experienced conflict and distress over prioritizing patient care vs their own safety, protecting family members from infection, and the reality that the supplies, medications, and equipment needed to save a life were not always available or were being rationed. Because of high infectivity, morbidity, and mortality associated with the spread of the virus, frontline health care workers were often in the position to be the only person at the bedside at the end of life with patients who were separated from their families. This is not how families should experience the loss of a loved one.4

There is a body of research regarding the long-term effects of moral injury among combat soldiers.3 It is reasonable to expect that feelings of guilt, shame, anger, and self-recrimination stemming from moral injury in these soldiers may be similar to feelings experienced by frontline health care workers during the COVID-19 pandemic and that their experiences increase the risk for acute stress reactions with long-term consequences including increased incidence of depression, anxiety, substance abuse, PTSD, and suicide.4,8 Behavior changes including intrusive memories, avoidance of situations that are reminders of prior events, self-isolation, and potential triggers of traumatic memories are common in individuals suffering from acute stress disorder or PTSD. Additional responses to stress, trauma, and moral injury include disturbed sleep, emotional changes such as numbing, desensitization, depersonalization, and a decreased capacity for empathy and compassion. For some individuals, the consequences of moral injury may be an opportunity for reflection and reprioritization of values and an existential inner process of reflecting on what is important in life.4

Given the consequences of moral injury, it is important for mental health professionals and health care providers treating frontline health care providers to recognize and identify those experiences that have the potential for promoting resilience.9

An analysis of data from 2,579 frontline health care workers in New York City early on in the pandemic showed that key factors predictive of psychological resilience were positive emotions, self-efficacy, purpose in life, strong social support, and not engaging in maladaptive coping strategies (eg, substance abuse).9 Psychological resilience was described by the authors as, “the capacity to adapt and thrive while facing adversity or challenging circumstances,” leading to the question of how can institutions promote psychological resilience in frontline health care workers?9

Initiativespromoting psychological resilience are critical.10,11 Interventions identifying those at high risk for moral injury and in need of support in the form of psychological first-aid and psychotherapy have the potential of improving resilience. Kameno et al administered the short-form of the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale with 4 additional questions, 2 regarding sleep, 1 on appetite changes, and 1 on alcohol misuse, in health care workers during the pandemic.12 The researchers found that women and nurses had higher rates of affective symptoms compared to men and other medical staff, respectively. The researchers noted that early identification and psychotherapy may improve psychological resilience and reduce psychological distress in nurses at high risk for maladaptive coping.12

The need for institutional support, leadership support, education, and training is equally important. Leadership and management are challenged to identify those practices that address the needs of their respective health care workers.10 Survey findings on the expectations and needs of health care workers (physicians, nurses, advanced practice clinicians, residents, and fellows; N=69) during the first week of the pandemic at a single hospital identified the following 5 requests of their organization: hear me, protect me, prepare me, support me, and care for me.13 Management and leadership have the opportunity to promote resilience and show visible support for the health care workforce with unique initiatives to help reduce and mitigate the long-term consequences of moral injury and acute stress response.

Similar to triage protocols and models to meet emergent health care systems demands from unexpected disasters, there is a need for a multilayered mental health care response for frontline workers. Self-care and wellness initiatives have the potential to reduce the long-term consequences of moral injury. Ongoing support, skills training, psychoeducation, and wellness education regarding strategies to address and process the experiences of frontline health care workers are critical for healing the wounds of moral injury. Empathic sensitivity on the part of mental health providers and primary care providers is essential. Listening to “the story” and having the opportunity to process and reflect on the self-talk related to the experience of moral injury can lay the groundwork for healing.

Self-care needs should include the opportunity to seek out and have available a support system of peers and colleagues. All too often the experience of shame, guilt, and self-condemnation are obstacles to seeking self-help and lead to self-isolation. If allowed to process and reflect on those experiences, health care workers may be provided an opportunity for experiential growth and a redefinition of priorities personally and professionally.

Leaders in health care have the opportunity to create and foster a culture of open, nonjudgmental communication. In the face of unpredictable events such as the COVID-19 pandemic, natural disasters, and social and political unrest that impact health care delivery, strategies are available to promote mental health recovery and return to stability and wellness among frontline health care workers.

Catherine R. Judd, MS, PA-C, CAQ-Psy, DFAAPA, is an assistant clinical professor in the Department of Physician Assistant Studies at the School of Health Professions, The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, Texas.

1. Taylor WD, Blackford JU. Mental health treatment for front-line clinicians during and after the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic: a plea to the medical community. Ann Intern Med. 2020;173(7):574-575. doi:10.7326/M20-2440

2. Hossain F, Clatty A. Self-care strategies in response to nurses’ moral injury during COVID-19 pandemic. Nurs Ethics. 2021;28(1):23-32. doi:10.1177/0969733020961825

3. Borges LM, Barnes SM, Farnsworth JK, Bahraini NH, Brenner LA. A commentary on moral injury among health care providers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Psychol Trauma. 2020;12(S1):S138-S140. doi:10.1037/tra0000698

4. Watson P, Norman SB, Maguen S, Hamblen J. Moral injury in health care workers. Accessed January 4, 2021. https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/cooccurring/moral_injury_hcw.asp

5. Shahrour G, Dardas LA. Acute stress disorder, coping self-efficacy and subsequent psychological distress among nurses amid COVID-19. J Nurs Manag. 2020;28(7):1686-1695. doi:10.1111/jonm.13124

6. Lahav Y. Psychological distress related to COVID-19 — The contribution of continuous traumatic stress. J Affect Disord. 2020;277:129-137. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2020.07.141

7. Stovall M, Hansen L, van Ryn M. A critical review: moral injury in nurses in the aftermath of a patient safety incident. J Nurs Scholarsh. 2020;52(3):320-328. doi:10.1111/jnu.12551

8. Pappa S, Ntella V, Giannakas T, Giannakoulis VG, Papoutsi E, Katsaounou P. Prevalence of depression, anxiety, and insomnia among healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Brain Behav Immun. 2020;88:901-907. doi:10.1016/j.bbi.2020.05.026

9. Pietrzak RH, Feingold JH, Feder A, Charney DS, Peccoralo L, Southwick SM, Ripp J. Psychological resilience in frontline health care workers during the acute phase of the COVID-19 pandemic in New York City. J Clin Psychiatry. 2020;82(1):20l13749. doi:10.4088/JCP.20l13749

10. Krystal JH, Alvarado J, Ball SA, et al. Mobilizing an institutional supportive response for healthcare workers and other staff in the context of COVID-19: the Yale experience. Gen Hosp Psychiatry. 2021;68:12-18. doi:10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2020.11.005

11. Park ER, Sylvia LG, Streck JM, et al. Launching a resiliency group program to assist frontline clinicians in meeting the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic: results of a hospital-based systems trial. Gen Hosp Psychiatry. 2021;68:111-112. doi:10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2020.10.005

12. Kameno Y, Hanada A, Asai D, et al. Individual psychotherapy using psychological first aid for frontline nurses at high risk of psychological distress during the COVID-19 pandemic. Psychiatry Clin Neurosci. 2021;75(1):25-27. doi:10.1111/pcn.13170.

13. Shanafelt T, Ripp J, Trockel M. Understanding and addressing sources of anxiety among health care professionals during the COVID-19 pandemic. JAMA. 2020;323(21):2133-2134. doi:10.1001/jama.2020.5893

#9538. The Simple Drink Swap Linked To 41% More Weight Loss

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Swapping diet drinks for water could help people lose more weight.

Women with type 2 diabetes who make the switch lose around 41 percent more weight over 18 months than those who continue drinking diet beverages.

They are also twice as likely to achieve diabetes remission during a structured weight-management programme.

The findings raise a question about whether a drink’s calorie count tells the whole story about its effects on weight.

Sweet taste without the accompanying energy might influence appetite signals.

The results suggest that everyday drink choices could play a useful supporting role in longer-term weight management.

The research involved around 80 women who were overweight or had obesity, had type 2 diabetes and regularly consumed diet drinks.

Researchers randomly assigned them either to replace their usual diet beverage with water after lunch five times a week or to continue drinking it.

Both groups took part in a six-month weight-loss programme followed by a year devoted to maintaining their progress.

By the end, women assigned to water had lost an average of 6.82 kg, compared with 4.85 kg among those continuing with diet drinks.

The difference amounted to almost 2 kg of additional weight loss across the programme.

The water group also showed greater improvements in measures including fasting blood glucose, insulin resistance and blood fats.

Diabetes remission was reported in 90 percent of women assigned to water, compared with 45 percent of those continuing diet beverages.

Dr Hamid R. Farshchi, study co-author, said:

“It’s a small change with the potential for a big impact on long-term health outcomes.”

The brain may respond differently when a sweet taste arrives without the energy normally supplied by sugar.

In a separate experiment involving around 75 adults, participants reported greater hunger after consuming sucralose than sugar, and the sweetener altered activity in the hypothalamus, a brain region involved in appetite regulation (Chakravartti et al., 2025).

However, hunger ratings after sucralose did not differ from those after water, so the findings do not establish that sweetened drinks necessarily make people hungrier than plain water.

The mismatch between sweetness and energy might help explain some appetite responses, but whether it contributed to the weight-loss difference remains unknown.

The study was published in the journal Diabetes (Farshchi Nasr et al., 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9536. Million-Dollar Mac & Cheese

In my opinion, mac & cheese is a must-have on any holiday table. If you’re looking to take the classic from good to million-dollar-price-tag-worthy, then this is the recipe for you. My million-dollar mac & cheese is what happens when you decide to take basic mac & cheese on a shopping spree to the fanciest cheese shop you know and shower it with gold leaf. Showcasing a trifecta of bougie (and delicious) cheeses and a crispy, crunchy panko topping, this irresistible comfort food will take center stage on any table it hits.

The cheeses:Most of the great mac & cheeses I’ve ever eaten contain three distinct cheeses: a base melting cheese, a tangy cheese with some character, and a sharper accent cheese. For this million-dollar mac, I chose Pecorino Romano as my accent, but went slightly rogue with the other two and paired fontina and French raclette, which both melt well and have quite a bit of funk. French raclette is particularly great for a mac & cheese sauce since it becomes almost fondue-like when melted, giving you cheese pulls beyond your wildest dreams.

The combination of these three cheeses is worth that million-dollar label, so even if you don’t typically buy these cheeses, I urge you to seek them out for this mac. That said, if you absolutely can’t find them, you could try combining comté and Camembert or Gruyère and brie with the Pecorino to give you a similar result.

The crispy topping:With a dish as rich and creamy as this mac & cheese, a crispy, crunchy topping is key. Pre-toasting the panko in butter on the stove ensures a truly golden-brown, delicious topping, without the nail-biting broiler-watching session. Using a higher butter-fat European-style butter here (as well as in the sauce) brings additional richness, ensuring this million-dollar mac is as decadent as it should be. In testing, I found that the breadcrumbs on top of the mac didn’t brown much more when they were on top of the mac in the oven, but if you’re concerned about them getting too dark, you can always lightly tent the pan with foil.

The gold leaf topping is a fun way to cue the whole “million-dollar” thing, but it’s totally not necessary. Use it if you want, but don’t feel obligated!

Storage:Any leftover mac & cheese can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the microwave, covered, in 30-second bursts until warmed through or, if you have enough, in the oven in a covered ceramic dish.

#9530. Air Fryer Croque Madame

Want to treat yourself to five-star brunch without making a ton of dishes—or taking off your pj’s? Hack the classic croque madame by making it in the air fryer. Here, crispy toast is topped with an egg and smothered with ham, cheese, and béchamel for a simpler version of the classic French dish that will transform the comfort of your sofa into a fancy brunch spot in five seconds flat.

How is this a croque madame?A classic croque madame is a toasted ham and cheese sandwich that’s topped with a layer of béchamel, broiled until bubbly, and then topped with a fried egg. This air fryer version takes all those components—toasty bread, fried egg, béchamel, ham, and cheese—and reconfigures them into a form that cooks much easier in the air fryer. You might say it almost looks like a classic egg-in-the-hole, but don’t worry! If you close your eyes, you’ll still taste croque madame.

The microwave béchamel:There’s nothing wrong with making béchamel in a pot on the stove, but making it in the microwave means fewer heavy dishes to clean—and it’s also a great hack to know if you’re somewhere with limited (or no!) stove space. Rather than standing over a pot, whisking constantly, you’ll simply whisk the flour into the melted butter, microwave until it’s bubbling, then whisk in the milk and microwave again. Once it’s thickened, you can fold in the cheese. Though I don’t recommend microwaving after the cheese goes in—that’s a sure way to break your sauce—if it absolutely needs it, you can microwave it for very short bursts just till it melts together.

Make-ahead & storage:Once cooked, the air fryer croque madame should be eaten immediately. That said, the béchamel can be made 2 days ahead and stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator. I recommend gently reheating it before using. I typically do this in the microwave in 15-second increments, stirring in between—this prevents the sauce from breaking.

#9528. Why ‘Blackout Wednesday’ Has Become One Of The Biggest Drinking Nights Of The Year

Thanksgiving Eve is fun and nostalgic—but it can turn risky fast.

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Wednesday isn’t typically a massive night for restaurants and bars—but the Wednesday before Thanksgiving is different. Most people have the next day off, and college students or young professionals are typically back in their hometowns for the holiday. What better way to kick off the long weekend than to get off your parents’ couch and hit up the local watering hole?

That’s how Thanksgiving Eve came to be known as “Blackout Wednesday” or “Drinksgiving,” one of the busiest drinking nights of the year. A 2023 study found that in 2022, liquor sales grew by 156% and beer sales increased by 85% on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Cocktail orders surged by 69%.

DoorDash has even named the day one of the busiest for alcohol deliveries. Among 10 more traditional holidays like New Year’s Eve and July 4th, Blackout Wednesday ranks right in the middle. “As families and friends return home for the winter holidays, the day before Thanksgiving has become the fifth most popular day for alcohol delivery,” DoorDash’s website reads.

Going out in your hometown is prime time for idly snooping on people from high school, witnessing some truly unlikely pairings (Tyler and Kayla?!). It’s social and nostalgic, but it’s also a day when one drink can easily turn into one too many.

It’s not all fun and drinking games, however. This unofficial holiday marks the start of so-called “DUI Season,” with checkpoints ramping up before Turkey Day. Your risk of coming into contact with a drunk driver also becomes 55% higher than on average days.

Short-term risks of heavy drinking and blacking out include vomiting, seizures, depression, and accidental injuries, as well as next-day anxiety and depression. Long-term, recurring binges are linked to liver damage, high blood pressure, and mental health issues. Alcohol-induced blackouts can also occur more rapidly after just a few drinks, especially if you are taking certain medications, drink on an empty stomach, or have a low body weight.

It’s totally valid to blow off some steam (or get out of chopping celery), just plan it smart. With actually-delicious mocktails, non-alcoholic beers, and ride-shares, there’s very little reason to put yourself—or others—in danger, especially during the holidays.

Hosts and guests alike can benefit from making a plan for keeping everyone safe until well after New Year’s Day by providing plenty of non-alcoholic options at gatherings, opting in on a “Dampsgiving,” checking in with loved ones (and designated drivers) before they hit the road, and always making sure there’s a spot on the couch for anyone who helped themselves to a few too many eggnog espresso martinis.

#9525. White Meat vs. Dark Meat: Which Part Of The Turkey Is Actually Healthier?

The nutritional showdown nobody asked for—but everyone at Thanksgiving needs.

Every Thanksgiving, the table splits into two camps. There's Team White Meat, politely asking for "just a slice of breast, please." Then there's Team Dark Meat, already eyeing the drumstick like it's the last Pop-Tart in the box. It's basically Team Edward vs. Team Jacob, but with gravy.

Somewhere along the way, dark meat picked up a reputation as the "less healthy" choice. As a dietitian, I get asked about this a lot, especially the week of Thanksgiving. The short answer is that dark meat isn't the villain it's made out to be. The long answer is way more interesting, so grab a fork. Cranberry sauce optional.

The color comes down to a protein called myoglobin. Myoglobin stores oxygen inside muscle cells, and muscles that work steadily over long periods need more of it. On a turkey, that means the legs and thighs, which the bird uses to stand and walk around all day.

Domestic turkeys use their breast muscles far less, so they carry less myoglobin and stay pale. Myoglobin contains heme iron, which matters for nutrition. More on that in a minute.

So when you choose dark meat, you're eating hardworking muscle. That changes its nutritional profile in a few notable ways.

Both cuts are excellent sources of protein. A 3-ounce serving of roasted, skinless turkey provides roughly 24 to 25 grams of protein, whether it's white or dark meat. White meat edges ahead by a gram or two, but in practical terms, both will do the job.

If protein is a priority, either cut gets you there. No need to stage a dramatic family intervention over the drumsticks.

Skinless dark meat does have more fat than skinless white meat, typically a few extra grams per 3-ounce serving. Some of that is saturated fat.

Context matters, though. The difference amounts to a few grams on a single plate, not a massive gap. Keeping the skin on also adds more fat to either cut. A slice of breast with crispy skin can end up in a similar ballpark to skinless thigh meat.

Saturated fat and heart health remain an active area of research. A Cochrane systematic review found that reducing dietary saturated fat was linked to a modest reduction in cardiovascular events over time. That finding reflects overall eating patterns across months and years, though, not what you eat at one holiday meal. A few extra grams of fat from turkey thighs won't make or break anyone's health.

Fat also brings flavor and moisture, which is why dark meat rarely turns into the dry, sawdust situation that can happen to an overcooked breast.

Remember myoglobin? Thanks in part to its heme iron, dark meat generally contains more iron than white meat. Heme iron, the type found in animal foods, is generally absorbed more efficiently than the non-heme iron found in plants.

That's meaningful, because iron deficiency is the most common cause of anemia worldwide. It's especially common among people who menstruate, pregnant people, and young children. Turkey thighs won't fix a deficiency on their own, but they can absolutely contribute to your overall iron intake.

Dark meat also delivers noticeably more zinc than white meat. Zinc plays a key role in immune function, wound healing, and taste perception. Not bad for the part of the bird some people skip.

This is where things get fun, because each cut has its own nutritional strengths.

These B vitamins help your body turn food into usable energy. Vitamin B12 also supports nerve function and red blood cell production, and B12 deficiency is more common in older adults and people who eat few animal foods.

Neither cut offers a complete B vitamin package on its own. Together, though? They make a pretty great team.

Not really. It's just different. White meat offers slightly more protein and less fat, plus more niacin and B6. Dark meat has more iron, zinc, and riboflavin, plus richer flavor and a juicier texture. Both provide vitamin B12.

Neither one deserves a "good" or "bad" label. Health is shaped by your eating patterns over time, not by which slice you pick from the platter on one Thursday in November.

If you have a specific health condition, a registered dietitian can help you figure out what works best for you. For most people, though, the best turkey is the one you actually enjoy eating.

Pick the cut you love. Better yet, take a little of both. Dark meat isn't a nutritional compromise, and white meat isn't a punishment. They're two parts of the same bird, each with its own strengths.

So go ahead and claim that drumstick. Or the breast. Or both. Your plate, your call. Just save some gravy for the rest of us.

#9520. What Couples Married For 40 Years Do When Life Gets Hard

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.

They describe listening to each other, talking through painful subjects and sometimes having the same argument more than once.

The researchers suggest that this response grows out of years of knowing they can count on their partner.

In attachment theory, a partner can act as a safe haven, someone whose presence makes it easier to bear distress.

Getting through a difficult period together may deepen that trust, making it easier to ask for help the next time it is needed.

Dr Christian Heim, the study’s first author, and Dr Caroline Heim, study co-author, interviewed each couple together, asking each person to describe what had put their marriage under strain and what had helped them cope.

The 180 participants were born in 24 countries and, with a few exceptions, had been married for at least 40 years.

Around two-thirds of the couples described a threat they believed could have ended their marriage, such as the death or serious illness of a child, infidelity or prolonged periods apart.

Talking, listening and arguing accounted for almost a quarter of the coping responses the researchers recorded.

After an affair, some couples described arguing over it repeatedly, while bereaved partners sometimes waited for a moment when both felt able to speak.

One partner in an American couple married for 45 years recalled asking their spouse about the son they had lost.

“Can I talk about our son? I’m hurting. Is it okay to talk about it?”

Some partners described taking time to grieve separately before they were ready to turn to each other.

Around four in five coping responses involved leaning on the relationship, whether by drawing closer, persevering as a couple or giving up something one partner wanted.

The interviews capture what couples in lasting marriages felt had helped them, leaving open whether the same approaches would have helped couples who separated.

When partners see a problem as something they face together, they may spend less time working out who is to blame and more time trying to understand what the other person is going through.

A previous analysis involving almost 18,000 people found that coping together and helping a partner manage stress were both linked to greater relationship satisfaction (Falconier et al., 2015).

Some couples in the interviews felt that an illness, a bereavement or a family conflict had left them closer, even though the experience itself had been painful.

A British couple married for 60 years described how they got through a serious conflict with their in-laws:

The study was published in the journal The American Journal of Family Therapy (Heim & Heim, 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9514. What Does Gen Z Think About Political Polarization?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S. today. Gen Z, however, is less inclined than older generations to view it as a permanent fixture in American politics, according to research by students in the Stanford political science course Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead. Students found that Gen Z is more optimistic than any other age group about the possibility of bridging the political divide in America.

“Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” said Jadon Urogdy. “We have a bright future. Our identities and views are still malleable, and that’s exactly why this moment matters so much.”

Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.

Urogdy’s results were among many findings from Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead, a spring quarter course taught by Ashley Fabrizio, a Stanford alum and head of research at the nonpartisan think tank More in Common. Working with Fabrizio and her team, students created and conducted a nationally representative survey of 1,610 U.S. adults that oversampled Gen Z to provide a more granular look into their political attitudes and opinions.

Fabrizio, who has taught the course for three years, has found that working with students surfaces concerns that standard polling may miss. “If we want to know what Gen Z’s political beliefs and attitudes are, we should let our students, as members of Gen Z, use their intuition to decide what matters in a survey,” Fabrizio explained.

Working in small groups, students were allocated several minutes of survey time to explore topics such as the political influence of online content promoting masculinity—aka the “manosphere”—the religious revival in Gen Z’s lives, and their beliefs about the American dream. Fabrizio guided students step by step through survey design, showing them how to craft research questions, field the survey, analyze data, and, finally, present their findings.

Students also examined the academic literature on polarization’s effects in American politics, such as how it contributes to political gridlock, drives support for political violence, and erodes trust in American institutions.

“There are many legitimate divisions in politics over competing policies and values, but polarization often drives us apart unnecessarily,” said Fabrizio. “Young Americans will have to find their own ways of bridging partisan differences and overcoming misconceptions about one another. I hope this class helps students see the value of doing so and gives them a sense of agency in addressing polarization.”

Natalia Galperin was excited about the opportunity to run her own study from start to finish, a first for the Stanford undergrad majoring in psychology. She also wanted to expand on her prior work as a research assistant for political scientist Shanto Iyengar in his Political Communication Lab, where she studied the effects of negative political campaign ads.

For her research project, Galperin examined the role of social media in inflating Gen Z’s hostility toward people from the opposing political party, a phenomenon political scientists call “affective polarization.”

“We thought Gen Z would be more polarized and misinformed because we get so much of our news on social media compared to older generations,” Galperin said.

What she and her classmates found reveals a more complicated picture.

While Gen Z respondents who said they used social media daily or almost daily were more likely to dislike the opposing party, their scores were almost identical to those of other generations.

“We found that greater social media engagement is generally linked to more polarized views of political parties, and the effect is seen at similar rates across all generations, not just Gen Z,” said Galperin, who will be interning with More In Common this summer.

Practices to help campus communities connect across lines of race, faith, ideology, and more.

Galperin also wanted to know whether social media deepens the divide between what Gen Z thinks people from the other side believe versus what they actually think, a phenomenon known as “perception gaps.” In testing people’s perceptions on immigration, she found that Gen Z did not appear to hold wildly distorted views about the other side—findings that push back against the familiar narrative that being online warps a person’s perceptions of politics.

Taken together, actively using social media seems to harden Gen Z’s feelings more than it distorts basic facts.

The class also found a wide range of political viewpoints, including differences between Gen Z who identified as Democrats and Republicans.

For example, in Urogdy’s project, he and his teammates found that those who were the most confident that polarization can be reduced identified as conservatives and Republicans, while liberals and Democrats believed the opposite—a finding that Urogdy said tracks with prior research: A person’s view of government depends on whether or not their political party is in control.

Galperin’s team also found lower levels of affective polarization among Republicans and Gen Z overall, and Democrats who reported actively using social media daily have higher perception gaps on immigration-related issues than average.

Another student team’s project revealed further complexities. They found that many Gen Z respondents are more likely than other generations to attribute problems like the affordability crisis to systemic failures in democracy itself rather than to specific policies or leaders. In their data, a notable share of young people said the system itself “is not capable of doing its job,” signaling a deeper, structural disillusionment.

“I think we’re all exhausted by the political system,” Urogdy said. “There’s this underlying feeling that what we want isn’t being translated into tangible change, and I think that there’s this overall feeling that instead of having animosity towards people across the aisle, there’s an animosity towards the system itself.”

Urogdy is pragmatic about what comes next.

“We can’t say polarization will disappear if we will it away,” said Urogdy, who is majoring in political science. Now, he feels he has a better understanding of what kinds of solutions matter. If people are disillusioned with the system, surface-level fixes—such as messaging—won’t last, he said. Efforts need to be ongoing. “If Gen Z is still one of the most reachable generations, the answer is sustained civic engagement, where we can rebuild trust in the system while working to reform it. We have a long path ahead,” said Urogdy, who said he is optimistic.

Fabrizio, too, is hopeful. “Gen Z is inheriting a polarized nation, but they are inheriting deep wells of democratic vitality, as well,” Fabrizio said. “America has a long history of self-government, a robust civil society, and communities that remain deeply committed to democratic values. Gen Z has high standards for our democracy, but living up to them is within reach. I hope older generations will listen and be inspired by Gen Z’s vision for the American dream.”

This article was originally published on Stanford News. Read the original article.

Melissa De Witte is the deputy director for social science communications for the Stanford News Service. She attained an M.A. in Media, Culture, & Communication from NYU and a B.Sc. in Sociology from LSE. She was previously the digital communications manager for the Division of Social Sciences at UC Santa Cruz.

#9510. Does β‑Blocker Use Increase Depression Risk?

The association between β-blocker use and depression was investigated in a population-based observational study recently published in the journal Drug Safety.

While depression is often cited as an adverse effect of β-blocker use, there is limited evidence supporting this causal relationship. To better understand the association between beta blockers and the risk of new-onset depression, the study authors analyzed data from the UK population-based Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) GOLD database.

“We identifed patients aged 18-80 years with an incident depression diagnosis between 2000 and 2016, and matched controls, and estimated the risk (odds ratio [OR]) of depression in association with use of β-blockers,” the study authors explained.

Findings of the analysis revealed an increased risk of developing depression among short-term users of β-blockers compared with no use at all (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.91; 95% CI, 1.72-2.12).

Among short-term users, increased risk of depression was mainly restricted to patients with a neuropsychiatric disorder taking propranolol (aOR 6.33, 95% CI 5.16–7.76).  Patients on propranolol for a cardiovascular indication were found to be at slightly elevated risk of depression (aOR 1.44, 95% CI 1.14–1.82). Apart from propranolol, no other lipophilic β-blocker or hydrophilic β-blocker was found to increase the risk of depression.

Additionally, no association was observed between long-term use of β-blockers and the risk of depression (aOR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.85-0.94).

“Our findings suggest that the reported association between use of β-blockers and depression may not be causal but rather a result of protopathic bias,” the study authors concluded.

Bornand D, Reinau D, Jick SS, Meier CR. β‑blockers and the risk of depression: A matched case–control study. Drug Safety. Published online January 19, 2022. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40264-021-01140-5.

Healthy and versatile bowls that come together under a generous drizzle of addictingly creamy vegan chipotle tahini sauce.

A savory coconut creamy broth, swirls of chili oil floating on top, beautiful veg and cubes of flavor-soaked tofu, and a pile of steamy rice at your service.

A cozy, hearty, humble bowl of this Country Chicken Stew is waiting for you! Chicken, thick-cut bacon, navy beans, veggies, and fresh herbs all simmering in one big pot. It’s a good one, friends!

This Hot Honey Salmon is giving off major fancy-to-eat-but-not-fancy-to-make vibes. Spicy-sweet salmon coated in fresh garlic, stone ground mustard, sweet honey, and flecks of red peppers flakes. It’s a magical little number!

Harissa Chickpeas with Whipped Feta! Perfectly spicy/saucy/tomato-y chickpeas smothered in creamy, garlicky whipped feta and served with naan, lemons, and cucumbers. Your next weeknight wonder!

Easy Veggie Enchiladas! Saucy, cheese, filling, cozy, and packed with any roasted veggies you want. Super versatile and easy to make!

Guess what’s for dinner? Creamy, spicy, delicious red curry lentils, made in the Instant Pot.

Amazing Mushroom Bowls with Kale Pesto! Smoky, sweet, salt mushrooms (or tempeh!), caramelized pineapple, peppers, and dollop of kale pesto, all served over rice.

Sesame Beef and Broccoli! Full of protein, green broccoli goodness, and sticky-sweet garlic and ginger flavor. Perfect at-home takeout!

Creamy Thai Sweet Potato Curry – packed with nutrition! Our favorite easy, healthy, winter comfort food recipe.

These Roasted Cauliflower Hummus Bowls are LIFE-CHANGING. A bed of garlicky creamy hummus, piled high with spiced roasted cauliflower, and a speckling of fresh lemony tomatoes and herbs.

Spicy Shrimp with Cauliflower Mash and Garlic Kale – tender-sweet shrimp and smoky garlic kale over creamy cauliflower mash. The most DELICIOUS fake-fancy weeknight dinner!

Roasted Vegetable Bowls! Crispy tender roasted veggies, buttery avocado, all together in a bowl with a drizzle of green tahini sauce.

15 Minute Meal Prep Cilantro Lime Chicken and Lentils! The BEST easy protein powerhouse meal prep. Just 15 mins of prep and totally hands-off cooking!

Instant Pot Sweet Potato Tortilla Soup! A smoky, limey, tomato-rich broth with onion, garlic, jalapeño, crispy tortilla strips, and tender chunks of sweet potato.

These healthy chipotle sweet potato skins are stuffed with a chipotle-sweet potato filling, black beans, corn, and topped with cheese. SO GOOD.

Healing Bowls: turmeric sweet potatoes, brown rice, red quinoa, arugula, poached egg, lemon dressing.

Fall is for snacking, too! Here are some of my favorite healthy snacks – for myself, or for my kids’ lunchboxes!

#9508. The Overlooked Ways Love Shows Up in Urban Spaces

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Over the past two decades, my doctoral students and I have focused on studying love, care, kindness, and compassion in urban settings. Why? Because social science research on life in America’s cities is desperately incomplete. Much like the vision of urban life that permeates most of American popular culture, social science research imagines urban areas as sites of overwhelmedness, disengagement, social and moral crisis, threat, and violence.

But, as someone who has lived and worked in large urban centers—New York City, Chicago, Detroit, Istanbul—I know firsthand that urban centers are also sites of human virtue. People in urban contexts, including those living in high-stress, oversurveilled, underresourced communities, draw daily from deep wells of love, compassion, empathy, kindness, and generosity in the service of caring for each other. From holding doors open for one another, to offering seats on buses and trains, to stopping to help with directions, to paying unexpected compliments, city-dwellers create environments that are saturated with powerful but easily missed acts of care.

My former students and I have been eager to understand how love, generosity, and care manifest and operate in the hyperdiverse, densely populated, loud, fast-paced complexities of urban spaces. Through surveys and interviews, we have sought to understand how adults residing in big cities define love, how they see love being expressed, and their views of the cascading effects of giving and receiving care, generosity, and love.

We have learned that the decision to express love and care for others in large cities is not simply a moral or emotional decision. We offer two examples of the lens needed to notice the presence of love in cities.

First, we have learned that identities matter in experiences of compassion, love, and care between strangers. Urban dwellers’ identity (for example, race or gender), lived experience, context, familial, cultural, and legal systems’ realities work together to shape decisions about whether to extend acts of love to people you do not know. For example, Kehinde, a 26-year-old African American man living in a large, densely populated city, described his experience of giving and receiving kindness, care, and love in his city as shaped by how he navigates other people seeing him as a Black man.

“I will see folks all the time that may need a hand with their bags or crossing the street or just little things like that. And I take a second, hesitate,” Kehinde says. “I don’t want to scare them. I don’t want to come off as a threat.”

To get through these moments, Kehinde describes engaging in a practice of analysis and shape-shifting. Before he steps in to offer help, he assesses the environment and changes the way he carries himself so that people will perceive him as a possible helper rather than as a threat. He says: “I smile a lot more. My voice might change a bit.” He might shrink his body and keep his head down, to avoid seeming intimidating. After helping someone, he moves along without lingering. Reflecting, he acknowledges not being his full, true self in these interactions. “I have to realize I’ve been socialized—made to believe that this is what I need to do in order to navigate the situation.” Kehinde’s story highlights the point that identities matter in economies of care. The images and stereotypes that we construct about people come at a cost even in moments of compassion. Stereotypes affect who we perceive as deserving of care, concern, and protection. Stereotypes also inform our expectations about who can be trusted to help. Stereotyping is not unique to urban settings. But because urban settings tend to be especially diverse spaces, they create abundant opportunities to study how identities and the social scripts we hold affect the way that strangers care for each other across lines of difference. What Kehinde and others bring to the fore is the reality that the targets of stereotyping are aware of the ways that they are perceived. They learn that to be seen as helpful rather than as threatening, they need to read situations correctly, make adjustments to their approaches (e.g., keep “appropriate” distance), and exit situations strategically. Targets of stereotyping must strike a balance between their own deep-seated motivations to behave caringly and their desire to stay safe. For individuals like Kehinde, miscalculations can be costly. If, in the effort to behave lovingly and compassionately, someone is misidentified as a threat, that can lead to a range of consequences from being rebuffed and embarrassed to becoming the target of violence, arrest, or death. The end result is that people consciously or unconsciously learn the rules of engagement around helping strangers.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

A second lesson that has emerged from studying love in urban settings is that love lives in the built environment of cities. I highlight this lesson in my Positive Psychology in Urban Settings classes. Cities are often saturated with murals, billboards, and symbols that convey messages of love, solidarity, and belonging. As residents move through neighborhood streets, they may encounter signs prominently posted in shop windows or near the entrances of religious institutions that remind them that “Black Lives Matter,” “Love Is Love,” or “Immigrants Are Welcome Here.” People display rainbow flags and national flags from apartment windows, on cars, and in other spaces, declaring both their own identities and pride for and solidarity with those identities. The architecture of urban spaces may also play a role in expressions of love and care. In many urban neighborhoods, porches, stoops, and front steps serve as places of connection and care. Simple greetings (e.g., “Morning, baby!,” “You doing good?”) voiced by neighbors sitting on their steps serve as ways of spatializing love, care, and connection in urban landscapes.

I return here to my initial point. Our studies of urban areas are desperately incomplete and will remain incomplete until we more fully examine how various forms of human goodness—including love and care—flourish in urban settings. Likewise, our understandings of love and care will remain underdeveloped until we explore how these experiences emerge in the most densely populated, diverse, complex social structures in which people live. We will truly understand love when we understand how it is titrated through place, context, history, culture, religion, structures of power, identities, and a host of individual and relational factors. Urban centers give us powerful opportunities to know love.

Jacqueline Mattis, Ph.D., is dean of the School of Arts and Sciences at Rutgers University-Newark. She studies human goodness in urban contexts.

By focusing on culture, family, and community, Jasmin Brooks Stephens says we can support mental health in Black youth long before crises occur.

In three years, I lost five loved ones, my dog, my childhood home, and my sense of invincibility. What I gained was a deeper capacity for gratitude.

Couples who embrace their own “microculture”—pet names, inside jokes, and rituals—may be happier and more satisfied with their relationship.

#9507. Apple Crisp

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 29, 2026

Made this last night, and it’s now the whole family’s favorite apple crisp. Easy to make and very, very delicious!

I jotted this apple crisp recipe into the notes app in my phone several years ago, and I return to it every fall.

Jammy, cinnamon-scented apples baked under a heavy (and I do mean heavy) blanket of buttery crumble.

I remember first making this in our old kitchen for a late-October dinner party – I made wild rice soup and apple cider old fashioneds (unreal), and someone pulled out the guitar just as the smell of apple crisp was floating from the oven. Absolutely charmed. I obviously bonded with this specific apple crisp that night and it has been with me ever since.

Why it’s good, if you ask me: the caramely apple layer underneath gets properly jammy, the topping gets properly crisp – just enough to provide contrast, AND, and, and, where the two layers melt together in the middle is just pure fall magic. Soft, buttery, and delicious.

Apple crisp in general is very simple, and this one feels rustic, almost, especially if you make it in a cast iron pan, which I usually do. Is she making apple crisp or is she living out her dreams from Little House on the Prairie on a chilly fall night? We’ll never know.

Toss apples with sugar, cinnamon, and flour. This photo shows apples that have been thinly sliced on a mandoline. You can also dice them! Both delicious.

I stir it up with a spoon or fork, and then bring it together into crumbles with my hands.

It’ll turn into a beautiful golden crumble with a layer of jammy apples underneath.

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

This can work with or without peeling the apples. Personally, I don’t peel the apples – I am lazy, and I just can’t be bothered to mess with what is already a perfectly good fruit. The peels cook down the same way the apples do, so they become soft and unobtrusive in the apple crisp.

#9506. Pastina Soup (Italian Penicillin)

This soup is my new go-to when my family is sick. The broth here is AMAZING – light, flavorful, and nourishing. Absolute comfort food.

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 1, 2026

What an awesome soup recipe! The family loved it! It will be on repeat in our home especially with the kids asking for more!!! Thank you.

Like, slurp that savory broth and go back for a third bowl kind of good.

My daughter got sick last week, which means that our whole family got sick last week. And when I get sick, I lose two things: 1) my appetite, and 2) my interest in cooking.

This pastina soup truly SAVED us last week. It is:

I can’t say enough about how much I loved this last week. I sat down at the table with a steamy bowl with extra parm on top, and found myself repeatedly going back for “just one more scoop” of the broth over those tiny stars, even though I swore I hadn’t been feeling hungry just a moment earlier.

My girls were pretty excited about eating tiny star pasta with olive oil + Parmesan, while Bjork and I ladled the luscious broth over our bowls and finally tucked into some nurturing food for the first time in several days.

Pastina refers to the tiny star shaped pasta, which I found at Target, and the nickname Italian Penicillin refers to the healing nature of the savory broth – almost like a chicken noodle soup, but simpler. (And if I’m being honest, I prefer this to chicken noodle.)

I hope you are healthy and well, physically and emotionally. But if you’re not, this is comfort meal that has been serving our family so well lately!

I keep them real chunky, and I give them a quick sauté with olive oil before adding all the liquid just to get things extra fragrant.

I use water and Better Than Bouillon broth base.

Transfer to a bowl to cool down for a moment.

And then add them right back to the broth pot.

Source Notes: “Italian penicillin” is a nickname for pastina soup, or pastina (small pasta) in broth. It is playfully compared to medicine because of its healing vibe, being that it is a warm, nostalgic, nourishing comfort food. It originated with generations of Italian grandmothers and it has moved into the spotlight after becoming a popular trend on TikTok over the last few years. 🙂

#9504. One Familiar Item Of Clothing Scored Lowest for Intelligence — Can You Guess Which?

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.

Of the six types of clothing the researchers compared, track pants also received the lowest average ratings for trustworthiness.

Blouses topped the rankings for intelligence and trustworthiness but scored near the bottom for confidence.

Short skirts showed almost the reverse pattern, scoring near the top for confidence and lower than long skirts on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Short skirts also gave the strongest impression of sexual interest, showing how much people can read into a hemline.

Long skirts fell between short skirts and blouses on confidence, while ordinary trousers scored higher than tracksuit bottoms on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Onesies gave the strongest impression of happiness and scored about as high as short skirts for confidence.

White clothes suggested a happier wearer than grey clothes did, with black clothes coming last.

These examples show how the impression changes with the question being asked: a blouse came out ahead for intelligence, while a onesie came out ahead for happiness.

The researchers began by asking about 200 people what they thought clothes could tell them about someone and comparing their answers with traits examined in previous research.

They then gathered ratings on 5,000 photographs from online shops, covering five kinds of impressions: intelligence, confidence, trustworthiness, happiness and sexual interest.

Participants formed these impressions from photographs of the garments alone, without seeing anyone wearing them.

The results showed that who was doing the judging explained more of the variation in ratings than which garment they saw.

For example, one person might associate tracksuit bottoms with training for a race, while another might picture someone spending a Sunday on the sofa.

The researchers draw a parallel between judging people by their clothes and judging them by their faces:

“That is, much like inferences from faces, the inferred attributes often lie in the eye of the beholder.”

The study was published in the Journal of Computational Social Science (Rosenbusch et al., 2021).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9501. The Elephant in the Rheum – “Burnout” Among the Workforce

Feelings of stress, fatigue, and exhaustion – what is being described as “burnout” – have become a common occurrence among providers, including rheumatologists, with important implications in clinical practice. Various surveys and studies have reported a substantial prevalence of burnout (approximately 50%) among rheumatology providers.

Beth L. Jonas, MD, Reeves Foundation Distinguished Professor of Medicine and chief of the Division of Rheumatology, Allergy, and Immunology at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC), joins us on this episode to provide deeper insight on the issue of “burnout” from a clinical practice standpoint.

Read the full transcript of the episode here.

Beth L. Jonas, MD, is the Reeves Foundation Distinguished Professor of Medicine and chief of the Division of Rheumatology, Allergy, and Immunology at UNC.

A recipient of a 2015 Rheumatology Research Foundation (RRF) Clinician Scholar Educator Award, Dr Jonas has developed a novel curriculum in Rheumatology in the Foundation Phase at UNC. She is a clinician educator and has an active rheumatology practice, where she sees patients with a wide spectrum of inflammatory rheumatic disorders. She teaches rheumatology to medical students, residents, and fellows and is actively involved in curricular development to train both physicians and advance practice providers in rheumatology.

Dr Jonas currently serves on the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Workforce Solutions Committee. She has previously served as the chair of the ACR Committee on Training and Workforce and has served as co-chair of the ACR In-Training Examination Taskforce. She has served on the board of the Rheumatology Research Foundation as well as the RRF Scientific Advisory Committee.

Dr Jonas is a founding member of the Carolinas Fellows Collaborative (CFC), a group of program directors from the Carolinas who work to enhance the education of their collective trainees. Dr Jonas was honored as the ACR Distinguished Rheumatology Program Director in 2015.

#9500. Fall Freezer Meals #2

These Fall Freezer Meals have been SO helpful for us. The prep is shockingly easy!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 14, 2026

A few months ago, I discovered what feels like a little life hack.

I started spending an hour each month getting a few meals prepped for the month ahead. We’re talking just assembling stuff for my favorite recipes into bags and freezing it!

And I can’t tell you how much this system makes me feel like I have my life together! It’s the best.

The recipes this month are absolute family favorites for fall!

And they all have cook times for Crockpot, Instant Pot, and stovetop methods. 🙂

Hope these help make your life easier this month like they have for us!

Everything you need is right on them. I print the cards out and attach them to the bags so I don’t have to use my phone at all for the prep or cooking.

For the streusel: mix 4 tablespoons melted butter, 1/3 cup brown sugar, and 3/4 cup flour into small crumbles.

Spray a muffin tin with avocado oil. Fill tins two-thirds of the way full with batter; top with streusel.

Store muffins in an airtight container or bag in the freezer (or fridge). To reheat from frozen, microwave 45-60 seconds.

Remove chicken from the sauce and shred. Blend sauce until smooth. Add chicken back in. Serve in tortillas with all the taco fixings you want!

Add 1-2 cups heavy cream and 1-2 cups chicken broth (as needed). To thicken: whisk 2 tbsp. cornstarch with 2 tbsp. cold water; add and simmer.

Whisk 1 1/2 tbsp. cornstarch in 1 1/2 tbsp. cold water; add to bubbling pot and let simmer until slightly thickened.

Stir in 2 cups of fresh spinach and fresh cilantro just before serving.

Serve with rice and chili crisp. I also love this with cucumber salad (thinly sliced cucumber and red onion, tossed with vinegar, avocado oil, salt, and sugar).
