#9396. 12 common physical symptoms of anxiety (and how to ease them)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Anxiety doesn’t only impact your brain. Sometimes the first sign is your heart pounding for no clear reason, or a wave of nausea before a big conversation. You might feel dizzy, short of breath, or like there’s a knot in your stomach. You’re not in immediate danger, but your body is reacting as if you are.

This is what the physical symptoms of anxiety feel like. They can be alarming, especially if you don’t recognize them as anxiety right away. But your body responds this way for a reason, and understanding it can take some of the fear out of the experience.

Below we’ll look at the most common physical symptoms of anxiety, why they happen, and some ways to ease them.

Anxiety can affect your body before you've consciously registered that you're anxious at all. These are among the most common physical symptoms.

1. Racing or pounding heart (palpitations): A fast-beating or fluttering heart is one of the most recognized signs of anxiety. When your body senses a threat, it releases adrenaline, which speeds up your heart rate to pump blood to your muscles faster. This is useful when you actually need to run. Less so when you’re just checking your inbox.

2. Shortness of breath: Anxiety can make you feel like you can’t get a full breath, or like you’re slightly suffocating. Anxious breathing tends to be shallow and fast, which can lower carbon dioxide levels in the blood. This can feel scary, and anxiety is a common cause.

3. Chest tightness or pain: Muscle tension is a core part of the anxiety response and can be most noticeable in your chest, where you might feel tightness, pressure, or even mild pain. Seek emergency care if you feel sudden or severe chest pain, pain with shortness of breath or sweating, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw.

4. Dizziness or lightheadedness: Fast, shallow breathing can also leave you feeling faint or spaced out.

5. Tingling or numbness: Lower carbon dioxide levels in the blood can affect nerve signals and cause tingling or a pins-and-needles feeling in the hands, feet, or face. It can feel unsettling, but it’s usually short-lived. Numbness on one side of the body, sudden weakness, or trouble speaking needs urgent care.

6. Sweating: Sweating is part of the fight-flight-freeze-fawn response. Anxiety and stress can switch on your sweat glands even when you’re not hot, especially on your palms, underarms, and face.

7. Nausea or upset stomach: Your gut and brain are closely connected through the vagus nerve. When anxiety activates the stress response, digestion can slow or become disrupted. That can cause stomach upset, nausea, cramping, or an urgent need to use the bathroom.

8. Dry mouth: The stress response can slow saliva production, so many people notice a dry or sticky mouth when they’re anxious. It’s common and usually temporary, though it can make speaking feel harder than usual.

9. Muscle tension, aching, or trembling: Anxiety hormones prime your muscles to act quickly. Sustained tension without a chance to release can cause aching, stiffness, or subtle trembling, particularly in the hands, legs, or jaw.

10. Headaches: Tension headaches often appear with anxiety and stress. They’re typically felt as a band of pressure around your head or tension in the neck and shoulders.

11. Difficulty sleeping: Anxiety and sleep tend to make each other worse. Anxious thoughts and a body that’s physically on alert make it hard to fall or stay asleep. Poor sleep, in turn, can heighten anxiety the next day, which is how the cycle keeps going.

12. Fatigue: Anxiety takes energy because running the stress response tires the body, and poor sleep or constant tension can add to it. Ongoing anxiety can leave people feeling exhausted even without much physical effort.

Note: Some of the above symptoms can also point to a medical condition. If you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or symptoms that are new, severe, or don’t feel like your usual anxiety, it’s best to seek medical care.

Anxiety triggers the fight-flight-freeze-fawn response (also known as the stress response). When your brain senses a threat, it activates the sympathetic nervous system and releases hormones like adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones prepare your body to respond to danger. Your heart rate increases, your breathing quickens, your muscles tense, and non-essential systems like digestion temporarily slow down.

This response is useful when the threat is physical. The challenge is that your nervous system doesn’t always tell the difference between real danger and everyday stress. A tense conversation can trigger a milder version of fight-or-flight. The result is a body primed for action in situations that don’t call for it.

For most people these symptoms rise and fall with the stressful moment. When anxiety is ongoing, the symptoms can stick around longer.

There’s no instant off switch for anxiety, but these approaches can help ease physical symptoms, both in the moment and over time.

Controlled breathing can help calm the nervous system, and research suggests slow breathing helps many people feel calmer. Slow, gentle breathing, especially with a longer exhale, can shift your body toward the rest-and-digest (parasympathetic) system, which counteracts the stress response.

Try: Breathe in through your nose for four counts and out slowly for six. Repeat for a few minutes. You could also try box breathing, where you rhythmically hold your breath between inhales and exhales.

💙 When your body needs help slowing down, we have a short, breath-focused session for you: Breathe to Calm Down with Chibs Okereke.

Grounding techniques can help pull your attention out of anxious thoughts and back to the present moment. The 5–4–3–2–1 technique is a popular choice. To try it, notice:

💙 If anxiety is pulling you out of your body, try Tamara Levitt's Grounding session on Calm, which guides you back to solid earth.

Exercise is well-known for easing tension, and you might find that even a short walk can take the edge off. Science agrees, with research suggesting regular exercise can help reduce anxiety symptoms over time.

💙 Not sure where to start? Try this Mindful Movement session with Mel Mah on Calm to bring gentle, non-judgmental awareness to your body as it moves.

Progressive muscle relaxation involves intentionally tensing and releasing muscle groups throughout the body. It’s designed to help you relax by encouraging each muscle to unclench. It doesn’t take long, with typical sessions lasting just 10 to 20 minutes.

Try: Start with your feet. Tense the muscles for five seconds, then release completely. Work your way up through your calves, thighs, abdomen, hands, arms, shoulders, and face. Skip tensing any area that’s injured or painful.

💙 Not keen on the tensing? This guided Body Scan Meditation moves your attention gently through the body, one area at a time, no clenching required.

Mindfulness practices train your attention to rest on the present moment rather than looping through worries about what might happen.

Mindfulness is something you build with regular practice. Over time, it can lower how strongly your body reacts to stress, which means the physical symptoms of anxiety may appear less often, or feel less intense when they do.

💙 Work through Calm’s Letting Go of Anxiety series, which is designed to help you sit with anxious feelings instead of spiraling.

Caffeine is a stimulant that can raise your heart rate and cause jitteriness, which may feel like anxiety or make it stronger.

Alcohol may feel calming at first, but it can disrupt your sleep and may make anxiety worse.

Cutting back on both is worth considering if you’re dealing with anxiety symptoms frequently.

If physical symptoms of anxiety are frequent, severe, or getting in the way of daily life, talking with a doctor or mental health professional is a good next step. Effective treatments exist, including cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and medication when appropriate. You don’t have to manage this on your own.

Physical symptoms are a common part of anxiety. Anxiety activates the body’s stress response, which causes real changes like a faster heart rate, muscle tension, and altered breathing. Many people with anxiety notice at least some physical symptoms alongside the mental ones. If they’re frequent or getting in the way of daily life, it’s worth talking with a doctor or mental health professional.

“Anxiety attack” isn’t a clinical term, but people use it to describe anxiety that builds until it feels overwhelming, usually in response to a stressor like a looming deadline or a tense situation. The physical symptoms can include a rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, muscle tension, trembling, dry mouth, dizziness, and nausea. These sensations can be distressing, but they tend to ease as the stressful situation passes or your anxiety settles.

💙 If you’ve experienced the symptoms of an anxiety attack, here’s how to recover and take care of yourself.

Some anxiety symptoms feel strange because the stress response affects many parts of the body at once. For example, fast breathing can cause tingling in your hands. Or you might have a feeling of unreality or disconnection (called dissociation). Muscle tension might make it feel like your throat is closing. These varied symptoms can all have anxiety as the common cause. Of course, if they’re new, intense, or don’t fit your usual anxiety symptoms, it’s best to check in with a doctor.

💙 Explore lesser-known symptoms of anxiety (some might surprise you!)

When symptoms hit, the quickest relief usually comes through your breath. Make your out-breath longer than your in-breath—for example, breathing in for a count of four and out for six—and repeat for a minute or two. A longer exhale nudges your body out of the stress response and toward its rest-and-digest state.

Grounding works too. The 5–4–3–2–1 method has you name what you can see, touch, hear, smell, and taste, which pulls your focus out of anxious thoughts and back to the room around you.

Anxiety can affect the body as well as the mind, and for some people the physical side is what dominates, with few or no obvious worries attached. Your stress response can switch on faster than your conscious mind registers what set it off, so a racing heart or churning stomach can come before, or even without, any clear anxious thought.

These physical symptoms are still part of anxiety, and the same tools, like slow breathing and grounding, can help calm them. If they’re new or unexplained, see a doctor to rule out other causes, such as thyroid problems, heart rhythm changes, or the effects of caffeine or medication.

It’s worth speaking with a doctor if your anxiety symptoms are new and unexplained, severe or getting worse, or affecting your day-to-day life. Some symptoms, like chest pain, shortness of breath, and heart palpitations, should be evaluated medically to rule out other causes, even if you suspect anxiety. A doctor can also refer you to a mental health professional if that would help.

If you’re experiencing sudden or severe chest pain, or chest pain with sweating, shortness of breath, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw, seek emergency care.

A worry loop is a cycle where anxiety feeds on itself. One anxious thought leads to another, and the more attention it gets, the stronger it grows.

For example, an anxious thought sets off a physical sensation, that sensation becomes the focus of fresh worry (“Why is my heart racing? What’s wrong with me?”), and the worry drives more symptoms.

Breaking the loop usually means addressing both the mind and the body. You can calm the body directly with breathing and grounding, or use cognitive approaches like CBT to interrupt the thought patterns that keep the cycle going.

#9395. Are Chimps Less Likely to Steal From Friends?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

In recent years, scientists have shown that chimpanzees favor certain peers by picking whom they prefer to groom and selectively sharing food. The behavior offers a glimpse into humanity’s prosocial evolutionary past.

But a question has lingered: How might a chimpanzee friendship affect antisocial acts?

In a new study that uses fruit as the loot, UC Berkeley researchers found that chimps steal less from their friends, and that friendship status affected the emotional expression of both victim and thieves. Closely bonded chimps swiped pineapple pieces from one another less frequently than those with weaker relationships. Additionally, victims were quicker to calm down when the thief was a friend, and thieves showed less hostility when stealing from a bonded pal than from a non-friend.

The new research deepens our understanding of the emotional underpinnings of our social lives, said Oded Ritov, the paper’s first author and a Berkeley psychology Ph.D. student.

“Collaborative relationships are important for our well-being, health, and survival,” said Ritov, who works with Berkeley’s Social Origins Lab. “Increasingly, we’re understanding that this isn’t something that’s unique to us, but that other animals have friends, as well.”

The paper was published online in September and will appear in the November issue of the journal Evolution and Human Behavior.

Scientists are sometimes hesitant to describe an apparently close relationship between chimps as akin to human friendship, arguing that we can’t grasp their cognitive and emotional complexity. To identify those who showed signs of a close relationship, researchers observed 26 chimps for more than 800 hours at the Ngamba Island Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Uganda. The team documented which chimps appeared to be closely bonded—like friends—by taking note of their grooming patterns, daily interactions, and how regularly they were within arm’s reach of others.

Then they set up two rooms. One contained a “victim” chimp with three trays baited with pineapple. Researchers attached a rope to the trays and led it into the other room, where a second chimp—the thief—could either leave the rope alone or yank it to steal the pineapple.

Chimps stole in 70% of trials with non-friends, compared with 61% of trials with friends. While 9 percentage points may not seem large, each chimp experienced both friend and non-friend conditions, a methodological technique that leads to a higher degree of confidence that the difference is meaningful and not just random chance.

“Ours is the first study to show that they’re able to hold back antisocial behavior with their friends,” Ritov said.

Researchers also measured how the victims responded to being stolen from by evaluating their stomping, fist-pounding, and screeching. Victims were initially angrier when friends stole from them but quickly moderated their feelings compared with when non-friends stole from them.

The thieves’ behavior also changed. When non-friends were the thieves, the thieves expressed negative emotions for much longer, suggesting they viewed the interaction as more hostile.

“This suggests that there may be mutual expectations in chimps from both sides of the friendship, which makes it seem more like the complex friendships we see in humans,” Ritov said.

Jan Engelmann, an associate professor of psychology and principal investigator with the Social Origins Lab, said previous work has shown relationship-specific intentions in nonhuman primates. But human friendships are about more than special intentions, he added—they’re about stronger expectations.

“We expect more of our friends,” said Engelmann, a senior author of the paper. “These findings really deepen our understanding of the evolutionary roots of friendships. This is, to my knowledge, the first evidence showing that also chimpanzees expect and maybe demand special treatment from their friends. These kinds of social expectations might form the basis of human moral principles.”

The paper adds to Ritov’s work that focuses on the evolution of human behavior and how morals and norms are part of our core being, traceable to other animals. He has recently studied whether nonhuman animals have a sense of fairness and is broadly interested in how emotions unfold across cultures and species.

“We think that these expectations might be the basic building blocks of the larger-scale cooperation we see in humans,” Ritov said. “The expectations that chimpanzees have from their friends or close collaborative partners might have scaled up to more generalized expectations for how we should treat each other.”

This article was originally published on Berkeley News. Read the original article.

Jason Pohl is a science writer in UC Berkeley's Office of Communications & Public Affairs.

#9394. The Common Vitamin Linked To Less Belly Fat

People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

People with higher levels of vitamin D tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

This deeper layer of belly fat, known as visceral fat, surrounds organs such as the liver and intestines.

It matters because people with more visceral fat tend to have greater difficulty using insulin to control their blood sugar.

The link with vitamin D became weaker when the researchers took body mass index into account, suggesting that overall body size could explain part of the difference.

One possibility is that vitamin D is spread through a larger volume of tissue in people with more body fat, leaving a lower concentration in the blood.

The researchers reviewed records from nearly 1,300 adults with type 2 diabetes who attended a hospital in Quzhou, China, during a two-and-a-half-year period.

Each person had a blood test for vitamin D and a measurement to estimate their visceral fat.

The researchers divided patients into four groups according to their vitamin D levels and compared the estimated area of visceral fat in each group.

The clearest difference was between the groups with the highest and lowest vitamin D levels, with the middle groups showing a less consistent pattern.

After accounting for BMI and other differences between patients, the researchers estimated that the group with the highest vitamin D levels had about 10 square centimetres less visceral fat area than the group with the lowest levels.

Earlier research using genetic data suggested that a higher BMI can contribute to lower vitamin D levels, with weaker evidence for an effect in the other direction (Vimaleswaran et al., 2013).

As well as being distributed through a larger volume of tissue, some vitamin D may be stored in fat tissue, which could affect how much circulates in the blood.

Everyday habits could also help explain why the two measures vary together.

Someone who exercises outdoors may get more sunlight and carry less belly fat, two differences that could help explain the link.

The hospital records did not capture how much sunlight participants got, how active they were or whether they took vitamin D supplements.

Since vitamin D and belly fat were assessed at the same visit, it remains unclear which changed first or whether both were influenced by other factors.

The study was published in the Journal of International Medical Research (Zhu et al., 2026).

The gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code. People hear "gift tax" and assume they'll owe the IRS money for giving a birthday check to their grandchild. That's almost never how it works. The federal gift tax exists to prevent people from giving away their entire estate during their lifetime to dodge estate taxes at death. For the vast majority of Americans, it will never cost them a dime.

Here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all. Give that amount to 10 different people and you've transferred $180,000 completely under the radar. Go above the annual limit and you still won't owe tax — you'll just file a form that tracks the excess against your $13.61 million lifetime exemption.

The gift tax is really a planning tool, not a penalty. Understanding how it works can help you transfer wealth to family members, fund education, reduce your taxable estate, and accelerate your heirs' path to financial independence — all without triggering any actual tax.

The annual gift tax exclusion is the amount you can give to any single recipient each year without needing to file a gift tax return or use any of your lifetime exemption. For 2026, that amount is $18,000 per recipient.

This limit applies per giver, per recipient. That means:

The IRS adjusts this amount for inflation periodically. Here's how the annual exclusion has changed over the years:

The annual exclusion has roughly doubled since 2002, when it was just $11,000. Inflation adjustments are made in $1,000 increments, so the number stays flat for a year or two, then bumps up.

This is the single most important gift tax fact: the person making the gift is responsible for any gift tax — never the recipient. If your grandmother gives you $50,000, she files the gift tax return and uses her lifetime exemption. You don't report it as income, you don't owe tax on it, and you don't need to do anything. Gifts received are not taxable income.

When you give more than the annual exclusion to any single person, the excess counts against your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption — currently $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples). You won't actually owe gift tax until you've exceeded this lifetime amount.

Let's put that in perspective. If you give your daughter $118,000 in one year, you're $100,000 over the annual exclusion. You file Form 709 to report it, and the IRS subtracts that $100,000 from your lifetime exemption. Your remaining exemption drops from $13.61 million to $13.51 million. No tax is owed.

At the 40% top gift tax rate, you'd need to give away more than $13.61 million over your lifetime before any actual tax kicks in. That puts fewer than 0.1% of Americans in gift tax territory.

Important sunset warning: The current $13.61 million exemption is set to be cut roughly in half on January 1, 2026, reverting to approximately $7 million per person (adjusted for inflation) under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act sunset provisions. This has created urgency for high-net-worth families to make large gifts before the window closes.

Several types of transfers are completely excluded from gift tax rules — no annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required:

The education and medical exclusions are especially powerful for the FI community. A grandparent can pay $50,000 in tuition directly to a university AND give the grandchild $18,000 in cash in the same year — all tax-free with no reporting.

If you give more than $18,000 to any single recipient in a year, you must file IRS Form 709 (United States Gift and Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax Return) with your tax return. Filing Form 709 does not mean you owe tax — it simply reports the gift and tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

One of the most powerful gift tax strategies available is the 529 plan 5-year election. The IRS allows you to front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts into a 529 education savings plan in a single year.

For 2026, that means you can contribute up to $90,000 (5 x $18,000) to a 529 plan for a single beneficiary in one year. A married couple electing gift splitting can contribute up to $180,000 per beneficiary.

The catch: if you use the 5-year election and then pass away during the 5-year period, a prorated portion of the gift returns to your taxable estate.

The gift tax and estate tax share the same $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Think of it as one pool of money that covers both gifts during your life and transfers at death.

Every dollar of lifetime exemption you use for gifts during your life reduces the amount available to shelter your estate from tax at death. However, there's a strategic advantage to giving during your lifetime: future appreciation on gifted assets escapes your taxable estate.

Example: You give your daughter stock worth $1 million today. You use $982,000 of lifetime exemption ($1M minus $18K annual exclusion). If that stock grows to $3 million by the time you die, the full $3 million — including $2 million in appreciation — is completely outside your estate. That's $2 million that will never be subject to estate tax.

The current $13.61 million lifetime exemption is scheduled to drop to approximately $7 million per person on January 1, 2026. For high-net-worth families, this creates a narrow window to transfer wealth at the higher exemption level. If you have a taxable estate anywhere near the future threshold, consult an estate planning attorney about accelerating gifts before the sunset takes effect.

A practical guide to making gifts without triggering tax.

Give up to $18,000 per recipient per year with no reporting, no forms, and no impact on your lifetime exemption. Married couples can give $36,000 per recipient using gift splitting.

Pro tip: There is no limit on the number of recipients. You can give $18,000 each to as many people as you want.

Payments made directly to educational institutions or medical providers for someone else are unlimited and completely excluded from gift tax. These do not reduce your annual exclusion or lifetime exemption.

Pro tip: The payment must go directly to the institution — not to the student or patient. Reimbursing someone for tuition they already paid counts as a gift.

Front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts ($90,000 individual, $180,000 married) into a 529 plan in a single year. The full amount starts compounding immediately.

Pro tip: If you die during the 5-year election period, a prorated portion returns to your estate. File Form 709 to report the 5-year election.

If you give more than $18,000 to any single person, file IRS Form 709 with your tax return. The excess reduces your $13.61 million lifetime exemption but no tax is owed until you exceed it.

Pro tip: Filing Form 709 is just paperwork — it does not mean you owe tax. It simply tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

If your estate is approaching the lifetime exemption threshold, work with an estate planning attorney. Strategies like GRATs, family LLCs, and intentionally defective grantor trusts can transfer wealth beyond the basic gift tax rules.

Pro tip: With the exemption sunset approaching in 2026, large transfers should be planned now rather than later.

In 2026, you can give up to $18,000 per recipient without any tax consequences or reporting requirements. Above that amount, you file Form 709 but still won't owe tax until you've exceeded your $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Married couples can give up to $36,000 per recipient using gift splitting.

No. The recipient of a gift never pays income tax or gift tax on the gift. The giver is responsible for any gift tax reporting (Form 709) and any tax that might be owed. Gifts received are not considered taxable income. However, if the gifted asset later generates income (like dividends or interest), that income is taxable to the recipient.

You must file Form 709 with your tax return for that year. The amount above $18,000 reduces your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption ($13.61 million). You won't owe any actual gift tax unless your cumulative lifetime gifts exceed the lifetime exemption. Think of it as paperwork, not a penalty.

Yes, though the amount matters. You can give $18,000 per year with no reporting. You and your spouse together can give $36,000. For larger down payment gifts, you'll file Form 709 and use some of your $13.61 million lifetime exemption — but no tax is owed. Your mortgage lender will require a gift letter confirming the money is a gift, not a loan.

No. The unlimited marital deduction means you can transfer any amount to your US citizen spouse completely free of gift tax and estate tax. No annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required. If your spouse is not a US citizen, a higher annual exclusion applies ($185,000 for 2026) instead of the unlimited deduction.

Gifts are not reported on your income tax return (Form 1040). If you gave more than $18,000 to any single recipient, you file a separate Form 709 (gift tax return) alongside your income tax return. The recipient does not report the gift on their income tax return either. Gifts are outside the income tax system entirely.

The gift tax affects far fewer people than most assume. With an $18,000 annual exclusion per recipient, a $13.61 million lifetime exemption, and unlimited exclusions for direct tuition and medical payments, the vast majority of Americans can give generously without ever owing a penny in gift tax. The key rules: the giver pays (not the receiver), gifts are not taxable income, and filing Form 709 is just tracking — not a tax bill. For FI families, strategic gifting is one of the most powerful ways to accelerate the next generation's financial independence while reducing your taxable estate.

#9392. Do art fairs care about non-VIP visitors?

Demonstrators confront police at the Place de la Republique. With more protests expected, Art Basel closed early as a precaution

October’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans. No other city could match the range and quality of the French capital’s art fairs and exhibitions, both at public museums and private foundations. And what about all those charming restaurants, cafes and shops?

“It’s important to be in Paris,” said Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October. “Paris is the undisputed capital of the art world—once a year,” Sharp added, speaking at Post-Fair’s preview on 19 October, in the chic Marais district. Nearby, someone had sprayed “mort aux riches” across the window of a bank.

The previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting. Further demonstrations, highlighting the neglected state of France’s secondary schools, the ever-rising cost of living and other grievances, had been planned in Paris and other French cities on the afternoon of Saturday 24 October. Unemployment in France for those aged 15 to 24 currently stands at 21.5%, almost three times the rate in neighbouring Germany.

On Tuesday 20 October, the day of the ultra-exclusive Avant-Première pre-preview of Art Basel Paris in the Grand Palais, the French activist collective Pillage de Classe (class plunder) posted a message on Instagram exhorting protesters to “take back” the famous Belle Époque exhibition hall on Saturday, the penultimate day of the week’s flagship fair.

Art Basel Paris has been held in the historic Grand Palais since 2024

Of course, the Grand Palais was not stormed, Bastille-style. In the highly unlikely event of protesters managing to “take back” the building, they would have been disappointed, just as revolutionaries had been in 1789, when they discovered the prison they had liberated contained just seven detainees. Art Basel Paris, taking no risks, had closed the event two days early on Friday evening (after an excoriating letter from France's gallery association to fair director Karim Crippa, Art Basel recompensed exhibitors 20% of their stand fees).

The mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth took even fewer risks, emptying its stand the day before, leaving three paintings by the local artist Hélène Delprat. The fair had been shortened to three VIP preview days plus just one day for the general public. Satellite fairs, like Paris Internationale and Post-Fair, closed at lunchtime on Saturday.

That Saturday afternoon, more than 100,000 people duly turned out to demonstrate. However, these proved predominantly peaceful and were confined by the police to the outskirts of the city.

The disruption in Paris had surely been a momentary blip. And Art Basel’s ultra-wealthy invitees, which the top end of the international art trade likes to call the “right kind of people”, had already been and gone. But what about the reputational impact?

“The collateral damage is substantial considering the whole point of being in Paris is to let yourself surrender to its myriad charms,” said Andrew Terner, a New York-based private dealer and collector, speaking in the immediate aftermath of the early closure.

The French authorities blamed “ultra-left radical groups” for the violence that had marred weeks of otherwise peaceful protests, begun in September by discontented teenage lycée students. Pillage de Classe is certainly a left-wing radical group; it views Art Basel Paris as a luxury playground in which art is used by the ultra-wealthy to protect their capital from taxation.

But maybe (leaving aside its desire to take the Grand Palais by storm) Pillage de Classe has a point, at least with regard to the fair’s top French clients. In France, the net worth of the country’s 500 wealthiest individuals has ballooned from 6% of the country’s GDP in 1996 to 42% in 2024, according to a much-cited article in the French business magazine Challenges. Tax reforms introduced by President Macron in 2017 excluded stocks, financial assets (including art) and corporate investments from wealth tax calculations.

Moreover, in 2003 the French government had granted tax breaks of up to 75% for private individuals and 60% for corporations that supported the arts. This encouraged investment in glitzy private foundations, such as the Fondation Louis Vuitton, François Pinault’s Bourse de Commerce, the Fondation Cartier and the newly opened Île Seguin luxury hotel and Large art centre, which have become such an alluring feature of the Paris art scene for international visitors. According to research by Apollo magazine, Bernard Arnault’s LVMH luxury group received an aggregate tax break of €518.1m between 2007 and 2017 to set against the €790m the corporation spent building the Frank Gehry-designed Fondation Louis Vuitton.

The ultra-wealthy have also grown a lot wealthier in the US in recent years. The share of the nation’s wealth held by the richest 0.0001% (around 200 individuals) is now more than seven times what it was in 1980, according to a November Substack posted by the Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman.

Today’s art market is dominated by the world’s wealthiest people buying the world’s most expensive art. Most of these people are pretty old. This is not a good look now that the Democrats have won a landslide victory in the US midterm elections, driven by a massive turnout of young voters. Authoritarian rulers like Viktor Orbán in Hungary and Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia have been voted out of office. Young people have been protesting en masse about their diminished life chances in France and more than a dozen other countries across the world.

Suddenly, ordinary people matter again. The young matter. But do they matter at art fairs?

Take ticket-pricing. In October, the general public were charged £48 each to attend Frieze London, with students being asked to pay £32. Does Frieze, which is owned by the billionaire Ari Emanuel, the former chief executive of the US entertainment conglomerate Endeavor, want to actively discourage young people from visiting? Or is that ticket price an acknowledgement that pretty much the only students who can now afford to attend the UK’s art colleges come from more affluent backgrounds?

The following week, Art Basel Paris, part of James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems investment portfolio, was charging €47 for a standard day pass and €30 for a student ticket. “The galleries pay for the fair. Visitors are a side business,” says Magnus Resch, a New York-based author and art market entrepreneur. According to Resch’s back-of-an-envelope calculations, stand fees generate at least €15m, while tickets bring in less than €3m. “Charging the public €47 isn’t about the money. It’s about keeping the fair exclusive.” (Art Basel does not reveal detailed breakdowns of its revenue streams.)

“It is important for the public to visit an art fair,” says Guillaume Sultana, whose contemporary art gallery exhibited on the upper level of Art Basel Paris, where footfall is slower than down on the ground floor among the mega-galleries. “But a lot of general visitors on the weekend are a bit frustrated because public tickets are very expensive.”

Sultana acknowledges that “the main business is done during the very first days of an art fair, always”. Despite the fair being truncated, Sultana describes the experience as “very good”, having sold a painting by the young Syrian artist Osama Al Rayyan during the preview for €15,000, among other works.

In the funfair-mirror optics of the international art market, €15,000 might appear a relatively “affordable” price point. But traditionally, sensible collectors have been advised to spend no more than 5% of their available wealth on art. So, whoever bought that Al Rayan painting, should, theoretically, have had €300,000 of spare cash available. For would-be younger collectors in today’s tough economic conditions, these are intimidating figures, unless they can call on the bank of mum and dad.

Collecting art is in serious danger of being perceived as something that old, rich people do. With so many established collectors ageing and selling, rather than buying, and a democratic wave pushing back against oligarchical wealth, this might be a good moment for the art market to think more about inclusivity than exclusivity, to take a broader view of who might be the “right kind” of people.

After all, who wants “death to the rich” sprayed across their gallery window?

#9390. How Artificial Intelligence Can Help With Critical Thinking

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving. Ironically, perhaps, recent research shows that people who interact with generative AI for work tasks can end up not thinking critically. They can surrender to AI’s quick and confident answers, which can lead to speedy but low-quality solutions.

Scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading. And they are showing that it can erode the very skills that make knowledge workers valuable.

My research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however. In one study, my colleagues and I interviewed 45 knowledge workers at a U.S. public university. They all were using generative AI applications in their core tasks: generating new ideas, solving complex problems, and designing novel solutions. We also analyzed the prompts and outputs from their iterative AI chats.

We found that when knowledge workers intentionally use AI to challenge their ideas—to generate friction—they can significantly improve their performance. Previous research on human-AI collaboration for loan evaluations had similar results.

Using AI to find information that contradicts your own can reveal unlikely perspectives that disrupt your familiar logic and spark new insights. This is particularly important because AI models quickly become familiar with how a user prompts the model and interprets its output, and the model presents information according to these patterns.

For example, a marketing professional in our study asked AI to create virtual customers with personas that would lead them to dislike a product under development, which was an accounting certificate program. The contrary feedback from the AI model revealed customer preferences that the accounting professional designing the program had not considered, such as using multiple cases from different industries to illustrate a principle, rather than cases from the same industry.

An attorney used AI to find obscure legal loopholes and to consider how companies might exploit them. That exposed surprising but realistic scenarios of hard-to-detect unethical behavior in employees.

Exploring unlikely and opposing ideas presented by AI can feel disorienting. To help, knowledge workers should lean on their own expertise to question surprising information that an AI system might provide.

An operations research scientist who works with supply chains described adapting unfamiliar computing programs from other fields suggested by AI, such as signal processing and wireless communication, which helped him create a stronger program of his own. Although the programs were new to him, his strong understanding of supply network modeling helped him see how he could apply them.

A study I was not involved with found that creative writers produce better copy when they use AI as a sounding board rather than to ghostwrite.

Knowledge workers can also use AI’s outputs to examine topics from multiple viewpoints, deepening their knowledge.

A research scholar in our study probed an AI system for journal papers that used a concept he was using, but in contrasting settings, which helped him understand the concept from different angles. A lawyer followed up on legal citations suggested by an AI model by asking for different types of illustrative cases. That helped her fully understand the original case and write a strong legal brief.

Leaders of organizations can encourage knowledge workers to develop friction-generating queries of AI models.

A straightforward approach is to use prompts that challenge rather than agree with a person’s thinking. People can also draw on their own knowledge, work experiences, and professional ethics to scrutinize AI outputs. Sometimes people realize that a response lacks originality, even if it is factually correct.

Organization leaders can also create programs for knowledge workers to share their experiences and insights. Regular sessions—led by cross-functional AI task forces or AI champions—can also help knowledge workers keep up with rapidly evolving AI tools.

Providing resources for knowledge workers is important, as well. Internal AI bootcamps and workshops led by AI experts or experienced users can help workers understand what AI tools can and cannot do.

A professor leading an initiative about AI use in teaching described how she developed internal competitions with prizes for professors who successfully completed AI bootcamps. Organizations can also offer AI sandboxes—safe, private environments where employees can experiment and learn how to use AI tools.

In these efforts to support knowledge workers, an important detail is pointing out that adding friction can appear to make an AI system work against you, but—as new research shows—it actually helps it work for you.

#9389. MCA Chicago receives gift of 65 works, most of them by women and artists of colour

Gary Simmons’s High Post (2013) Photo: Jim Prinz, courtesy MCA Chicago

A recent gift of 65 works to the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) Chicago honours the institution's upcoming 60th anniversary and its outgoing director, Madeleine Grynsztejn.

The philanthropists Jack and Sandy Guthman worked with the MCA’s curatorial team, poring through the couple’s extensive collection to choose the pieces. Grynsztejn got the selection down to 65, then hit a wall. Paring it down to 60, as originally intended, became an excruciating process. The Guthmans, champions of the MCA for decades, did not force the museum to choose just 60.

Grynsztejn considers this an extraordinary model for what can happen when a museum and philanthropists are in alignment. To date, the Guthmans have donated 130 works to the MCA—the largest donor gift in the museum’s history.

For Grynsztejn, building a great museum collection takes not only visionary leadership but visionary philanthropy. “The Guthmans have invested in Chicago artists, making their gift one that also has a civic impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. Included in the gift is work by Amanda Williams, Dawoud Bey and Rashid Johnson.

The Guthmans have spent decades supporting Chicago’s civic and cultural institutions. As a real estate lawyer, Jack started out by providing pro bono services. Meanwhile, Sandy directed her family’s foundation Polk Bros. Jack was elected as a trustee of the MCA in 1989 and currently serves on its board. For the MCA’s 50th anniversary, the couple donated 50 photographs by women artists.

Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995–96) Photo: Nathan Keay, © MCA Chicago

The current gift includes 23 pieces by artists of colour and 19 by women. Thirteen artists are new to the MCA’s collection, including Mohamed Bourouissa, James Casebere, Julia Fish, Christian Marclay, Adrian Paci, Elle Perez and Shinique Smith. Other gifts, like photographs by Bey, deepen the MCA’s holdings.

“In some cases, we are adding an entirely new collection,” Grynsztejn says, referring to Bey’s early photography in Harlem, “and in some cases, we are gaining an icon, as in Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995-96).”

The MCA began as a kunsthalle in 1967. It started receiving gifts, so in 1974 it formalised its collection. Despite the fact that the very first piece to enter the MCA’s collection was by Marisol, it eventually began to reflect the usual gender and racial biases.

During her tenure, Grynsztejn has sought to change that by establishing the Women Artists Initiative, inspired by the experience of many colleagues who have found it more challenging to fundraise for exhibitions by women artists. The museum’s proof-of-concept came with the success of exhibitions by Faith Ringgold, followed by a traveling Yoko Ono retrospective. The MCA has added women artists to the collection at four times the national average. Recently, the initiative has been renamed the Madeleine Fund for Women Artists and now has a $5m endowment.

Since Grynsztejn’s arrival at the museum in 2008, the MCA’s collection has grown from approximately 1,300 to 3,800 works. At least half of the acquisitions under her leadership have been by women and artists of colour. “This is not woke or [diversity, equity and inclusion],” she says. “It’s good business and good culture. Because if you are a public trust, you are in service to your public.”

Government funding for the Sydney institution, which is already closed one day a week and is now charging A$20 entry, remains the same as in 2008

This ups the museums holdings of the artist to 22

The gifted works are predominantly by woman-identifying and Bipoc artists, including pieces by Huma Bhabha, Arthur Jafa, Adrian Piper, Jennie C. Jones and Cindy Sherman

#9388. What My Son Is Learning From Artificial Intelligence

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

My 10-year-old son came to me recently with a question about black holes. Not in the way children usually do, restless and easily redirected, but with the focused intensity of someone who had already been thinking for a while.

He had been talking to an artificial intelligence—specifically, a large language model called Claude.

I looked at their conversation. It had been good, I discovered. The explanations were patient and well-calibrated. He had followed up, pushed back, and received answers that adjusted to his level. By the time he found me, he was genuinely engaged, asking the kind of questions that suggest a mind that is curious and actively at work.

But I have also been watching something else. It is not that he looks things up. Children with questions about black holes have always turned outward, to books or to a particularly knowledgable parent or teacher. What has changed is the speed. When the uncertainty is of a sort that once had to be lived with for a while, my son reaches for an answer sooner than he used to. The question is no longer something to sit with. It is something to resolve. And I find myself wondering what this means about his relationship to sitting with not knowing.

That shift, subtle as it is, may point to something worth taking seriously.

I am a psychoanalyst, and I spend my professional life attending to what develops in the space between people, including what develops when that space is too quickly filled.

Childhood has always involved productive friction. Not knowing how something works, waiting for an answer, trying to figure something out without immediate resolution. These experiences are not incidental to development, but are part of how the mind learns to tolerate uncertainty, to hold a question open, and to struggle toward understanding. The capacity to sit with not-knowing is itself a developmental achievement that underlies creative thinking, emotional regulation, and the ability to navigate a world that rarely resolves cleanly.

I watched this in miniature not long ago. My son was waiting for a package—a computer part he had saved for—and the delivery had been delayed by weather. In an earlier childhood, mine perhaps, this would have been a long afternoon of checking the window. Instead he opened a chat to resolve the uncertainty: how long do weather delays usually last, what determines them, how do you read the tracking data from the delivery company to get the most accurate picture. The conversation was detailed and as far as I could tell the information was reliable. He came away with a small expertise in logistics, but with an estimate that turned out, in the end, to have no relation to anything. The package arrived that evening, on none of the schedules he had so carefully worked out with the help of his AI tool.

The point is not that the AI was wrong, because predicting a delayed truck is difficult. The point is instead that waiting, the old childhood experience of wanting something that has not yet come, was converted into a research problem that could be managed instead of endured. I admired his resourcefulness tremendously and am grateful he had the opportunity to think through a complex problem. I also found myself wondering what the afternoon would have asked of him without it.

AI reduces precisely this sort of friction. It does so efficiently and often helpfully. But consistently removing the experience of not-knowing from a developing mind is not a neutral act. It shapes what the mind comes to expect of itself.

The research on what this does to thinking is new, and the majority of it is about adults. Despite this, it points in a consistent direction. In one widely discussed study from the MIT Media Lab, not yet peer-reviewed, adults who wrote essays with ChatGPT showed weaker and less distributed patterns of brain connectivity than those who wrote without its assistance, and many struggled after writing to quote sentences they had just produced. The researchers called the pattern “cognitive debt.”

Another study, a survey of 666 adults, found that heavier reliance on AI tools was correlated with weaker critical thinking, most pronounced in its youngest participants. The author suggested this might result from the offloading of mental effort itself. None of this is certain but is, instead, a suggestive pattern of early evidence. And the transfer to children is not straightforward. An adult who offloads mental effort has already built the capacity being offloaded; a child is still building it. Does that make the effect smaller in children or larger and more durable? We do not know.

This is different from what smartphones have done. The concern with smartphones has been largely about attention and social life: what children see, how they spend time, how they relate to each other. These are real and serious concerns, but AI introduces a different kind of change. It is not just another screen competing for a child’s focus. It is something closer to an interactive presence that responds, explains, adjusts, and, crucially, never gets tired.

For a developing child, this matters in a way we have not yet fully come to terms with.

Children learn who they are through relationships with other minds. This process is not primarily cognitive but unfolds through the experience of being known and misunderstood, challenged, surprised, and pushed back against. Through encounters like these, children discover that other people have their own inner lives, including their own perspectives and their own limits. They learn how to navigate the gap between what they expect and what they receive from others. Over time, these negotiations, internal and external, form the scaffolding of a self.

What is distinctive about AI, from a developmental standpoint, is not that it is wrong, or distorting, or even necessarily harmful. It is that it is extraordinarily responsive without having genuine subjectivity. It simulates the experience of being understood without the reality of another mind behind it.

For an adult, this distinction is available, if sometimes quite easy to forget. For a child, whose capacity to distinguish between a mind that truly has an inner life and one that simulates having one is still forming, the distinction might not yet be fully available at all.

Researchers have begun to observe how children try to think this problem through in real time. In one University of Edinburgh study of families with smart speakers, primary-school children were observed probing whether the device in the kitchen had a mind of its own, settling, provisionally, on conclusions like the one that gave the study its title: “Alexa doesn’t have that many feelings.” That, however, was a machine that talks in highly scripted phrases, in contrast to the systems children now converse with which are fluent and personal, attuned to the shape of a particular child’s interactions. Working out what this means has become correspondingly harder.

This creates something new in the developmental landscape. When a child turns to AI in a moment of confusion or distress and receives a fluent, patient, seemingly attuned response, the attachment system is engaged. The child feels, in some functional sense, heard. And that feeling, whatever its source, is real in its effects.

I have not seen my son turn to AI for emotional support, and I am glad for that, because here the questions are harder still. These systems shape themselves to their user. They adopt your vocabulary, match your register, remember what concerns you, and are available at three in the morning without complaint. Nothing in the design pushes back, for the most part, or asks anything of you. It would be difficult to engineer an arrangement better suited to engaging the attachment system of a child who is lonely or lacking in the structure needed for sound development.

The early numbers suggest that many children have already found their way there. In a national survey released by Common Sense Media in 2025, nearly three in four American teenagers had used an AI companion, and about a third had chosen to discuss something serious with an AI instead of with a person. A similar share described their AI conversations as at least as satisfying as conversations with friends.

In the United Kingdom, the nonprofit Internet Matters found that roughly one in eight children who use chatbots do so because they have no one else to talk to. The American Psychological Association was concerned enough to issue a health advisory in 2025, noting that adolescents are less likely than adults to question the accuracy or the intent of what a machine tells them, and warning that simulated companionship may begin to displace the relationships in which development actually happens.

For a child without reliable support, the relief such a system offers may be real, and so I am reluctant to dismiss it. But relief is not the substance of attachment. A full attachment relationship requires another person who can be truly changed by you, and with you—someone who is affected, who has limits, who gets things wrong and can be held to account. An AI can extend the experience of being emotionally met indefinitely. What it cannot do is be moved.

For the child who is largely or completely unattended to, this may still be better than nothing at all. Soothed in the early hours of the morning, a child whose sadness before bed is registered somewhere may be kept afloat by something real, and I would not wish to take it from her. But we should be honest about such an arrangement, which I expect will become increasingly common. It is a patch and not a structural solution. When a machine becomes the most reliable attention in a child’s life, the pertinent question is not about the machine but about the deprivation that made it necessary. And, crucially, a culture that responds to unattended children with software is treating the symptom while leaving the underlying structure intact.

There is also a quieter concern about authority and accountability.

Children have always learned to navigate between competing sources of knowledge, including parents, teachers, peers, and books, each with their own perspective, their own limits, and their own accountability. This navigation is itself developmental. The child who discovers that a parent doesn’t know something, or that a teacher can be wrong, or that a friend sees things differently, is developing a more differentiated relationship to knowledge.

AI, in the form a child is most likely to reach on their own, enters this landscape as something that appears to know a great deal, that expresses itself with fluency and confidence, and that has no stable point of view and no accountability for what it says. When a child asks why a friendship went wrong, or whether they were right to feel hurt, the answer they receive may shape the story they tell themselves about what happened. And unlike a parent or teacher, the system may not challenge the child’s assumptions so much as elaborate them. None of this is inherent to the technology under discussion. A system can be built to hold a position and to answer for it, but the ones children use are mostly not built that way.

Children appear to be taking up the offer. The same Internet Matters report found that nearly two-thirds of British children between nine and 17 had used an AI chatbot; among those who had, roughly a quarter had asked one for advice—on schoolwork, but also on more personal matters—and four in 10 expressed no reservations about following the advice they received.

None of this means that AI in children’s lives is a mistake. The benefits my son has experienced are genuine—wider curiosity, more sophisticated questions, greater confidence in exploring unfamiliar terrain. These are real, and they matter.

Tom Wooldridge is the author of the new book End the Food Fight: Replacing Control with Connection to Help Your Child Heal from an Eating Disorder (Guilford Press, 2026, 140 pages).

Some of what he brings home delights me. He asked recently whether you could power a sailboat by blowing into the sail through a straw. The answer he received was better than the one I would have managed: blowing at your own sail from on board mostly cancels itself out, since you push the air forward and the air pushes you back. Mostly, but not entirely—if the sail catches the stream and turns it around, a little net thrust survives, and if you skip the sail altogether and aim the straw backward, you have built yourself a very small jet engine. He spent the rest of the day on propulsion: rockets, squid, the reason a fan bolted to a sailboat is an old physics puzzle with a surprising answer.

But development is not only about access to knowledge. It is also about the conditions under which a self forms—conditions that include, crucially, the experience of not knowing, of waiting, of struggling toward understanding without guarantee of arrival. These are not inefficiencies to be optimized away. They are the medium through which a mind learns what it is capable of. A child who has never had to sit with a question—who has always had access to a patient, fluent, endlessly available presence to resolve it—may be acquiring knowledge without acquiring the tolerance for uncertainty that makes knowledge genuinely usable.

This is the thing I find myself returning to when I watch my son. He is, in many ways, more intellectually alive than he might otherwise be. He explores further and asks better questions. At the same time, when uncertainty arises, he reaches outward more quickly than he used to—to a presence that is always available, always patient, always responsive. What I cannot yet know is what he is quietly learning to expect: from knowledge, from relationship, and from himself.

We are not conducting a study. We are raising children. And the conditions of childhood have changed again, in ways whose full significance has not yet come into view.

Tom Wooldridge, Psy.D., is a psychoanalyst, founding dean of the School of Psychology at Golden Gate University, and director of the Human Systems Lab, which explores the roles of AI and other emergent technologies in human systems.

#9387. Weight Loss: A Half Cup Of This Food Reduces Belly Fat

Reduce your belly fat 10 percent with a half cup of this food.

Reduce your belly fat 10 percent with a half cup of this food.

Lowering sugar consumption by about one can of soda and adding one half-cup of fibre-rich foods daily reduces abdominal fat and type 2 diabetes risk.

A study has found that decreasing about 47 grams of sugar intake per day — equivalent to a can of soda — lowers insulin secretion, on average, by 33 percent.

Increasing fibre intake by 5 grams a day — the amount in a half cup of beans — results in a 10 percent reduction of belly fat.

Visceral fat is a type of body fat stored within the abdominal area and internal organs.

This type of fat causes abdominal obesity and is also associated with several health problems, like type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and cancer.

Dr Emily Ventura and colleagues conducted a 16-week study on overweight Latino adolescents who were between 12 to 19 years old.

They tested if increasing fiber consumption and decreasing sugar intake have an effect on type 2 diabetes risk factors.

“A reduction in visceral fat indicates a reduction in risk for type 2 diabetes, considering that to a greater degree than total body fat, visceral fat [fat surrounding the internal organs] has been shown to be negatively associated with insulin sensitivity.”

Those who increased fiber intake had a significant reduction in body mass index (-2 percent vs. 2 percent) and visceral adipose tissue (-10 percent vs. no change) compared with those who decreased fiber intake.”

Being overweight or obese are serious issues affecting adults and children around the world.

The World Health Organization reports that in 2016 over 1.9 billion adults were overweight and more than 650 million adults were obese.

“Our results suggest that intensive interventions may not be necessary to achieve modifications in sugar and fiber intake.

Accordingly, nutritional guidance given in the primary care or community setting may be sufficient to promote the suggested dietary changes in some individuals.

In addition, policies that promote reduced intake of added sugar and increased intake of fiber could be effective public health strategies for the prevention of type 2 diabetes in this high-risk population.”

The study was published in the Archives of Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine (Ventura et al., 2009).

#9386. How Do You Raise Kids to Be Emotionally Mature?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Raising a teen is one of the last chapters in parenting. During these years, it’s easy to prioritize your child’s grades, sports, and other accolades, especially as they inch toward leaving the nest.

While achievement is one marker of success, there’s another (often overlooked) skill that shapes your teen’s well-being and development: emotional maturity.

According to clinical psychologist Lindsay Gibson, emotional maturity develops through deep emotional connections, beginning with a child’s parents and primary caretakers. Research shows emotional maturity is the ability to accept and express care, temper big feelings, and make wise choices. Without it, teens are more likely to feel lonely and less satisfied with life, one study found.

In her latest book, How to Raise an Emotionally Mature Child, Gibson points out that “the quality of humanity’s future depends on the emotional maturity of coming generations.”

Juli Fraga: In your book, you mention that humanity’s future will depend on emotional maturity. Why does this matter so much right now?

Lindsay Gibson: Emotional maturity is critical to our well-being as individuals and to the smooth, productive, and innovative aspects of society. When you’re emotionally mature, you can think and anticipate consequences. You can also look back and learn from what you’ve done before. So, you can rely on your thinking to help you deal with reality. Emotional maturity also means tuning into your inner world, including your emotions, imagination, hopes, dreams, connections to other people, and sense of belonging.

JF: Our society places a lot of emphasis on achievement, and less importance on emotional intelligence. How can parents help their teens balance the two?

LG: There’s a real cultural pull in society to prize intelligence and achievement. But when parents get too fixated on these qualities, a child may feel like performance matters more than their thoughts, feelings, and sense of safety.

Kids need to be safely held and supported through the growing-up process. It helps them feel resilient, secure, and confident—qualities they need to take out into the world to function independently. If you get too fixated on the intelligence and achievement parts, you’ve got someone who’s very powerful in one area, but whose emotional side may be underdeveloped. It’s the balance between the two that matters.

JF: In your book, you mention why it’s so important for parents to help their kids develop a sense of self. Can you explain why this matters, especially during the teen years when kids are individuating?

LG: One way teens find out who they are is by discovering who they’re not. Teens might push a limit or break a rule, and it’s all par for the course. What’s important for parents is to be able to recognize and imagine that their child has a separate heart and mind from theirs—a process called “mentalization.”

A self is that inner spark that speaks to us. It says “don’t do that” or “now’s the time to go for it.” It guides you toward what’s most compatible with your individuality and who you are meant to be.

Our sense of self comes from our relationships with people we love and who love us. To feel secure, kids need solid, dependable, connected, and deeply resonant relationships with their parents and caretakers. They need parents who are curious and reflect something back that’s meaningful about who the young person is. When they have that foundation, they have a sense of being a real person inside.

JF: Parents are so busy these days, and overloaded—mentally and emotionally. Raising emotionally mature kids may feel like another big to-do on an already long list. What advice do you have?

LG: Taking time to pause and take your child seriously as a real person will work wonders for their self-confidence and future resilience.

Slowing down takes practice because by the time you’re old enough to have a family, you’ve probably been very goal-directed; parents can be pretty hard on themselves because our culture is so fixated on achievement.

But pulling yourself away from your goal for even a second to tend to your child is something worth practicing because that’s what children’s needs are all about. Kids also develop confidence when they know they matter just as much as anybody else.

JF: What are some behaviors that are normal for teens but that parents might misinterpret as pushback or misbehavior?

LG: Sometimes teens experiment with saying or doing things that clash with their socialization up to that point, such as the language they use or the clothes they wear. These are things that the parent can feel like, “Whoa, I’m uncomfortable with this…”

Here are two meaningful ways to navigate these moments.

Ask your teen questions about what they’re into, such as the styles they like or what they admire about someone they idolize. Try showing interest, not intrusive interest, but just interest in what they like, or why they are experimenting with different things.

Keep in mind that when your teen snaps at you, is in a bad mood, or slams the door, their emotional centers are activated in a way that will probably never be repeated in their life because their brains prioritize emotional development first during this stage.

JF: Can you share more about why a teen’s development follows this trajectory?

LG: Yeah, I know it’s easy to ask, “Why in the world would nature do it that way?” It’s because that’s how important the emotional self and relationships are to our real success as independent adults.

As adults, we have to know ourselves inside and out and use our feelings to guide us. Teens are still trying to work this out. Learning how to handle these emotions takes a lot of practice. They’re finding out what it’s like to feel rage, or what it’s like to be in love, or to feel disappointed. And they’re feeling them in the most intense way they ever will, because the brain is taking on the job of developing them into a really deep, complete human being.

JF: What advice do you have for parents when their teen’s emotions push their own buttons?

LG: Keep in mind that when your teen responds in an adamant, emotional, defiant way, or calls you names, they’re not really in command of those emotions yet.

Instead of coming down hard with words that suggest they’re not a good person, try to respond with: “I’m really interested in how you feel about this. I want to hear your arguments, but when you call me a name, it makes it impossible for me to be available to you. It just doesn’t work. We don’t call each other names in this family. That won’t work when you’re an adult, either.”

The interaction then becomes an education about how people respond to different kinds of approaches. Harshness that stops a teen cold shuts down their impulse to communicate their feelings to other people, which isn’t good for resilience or honest relationships.

JF: What are two things that parents do to foster emotional maturity that can actually backfire?

LG: One is the importance of achievement, of having a good resume. Of course, parents know how hard life is as an adult. We feel it’s our duty to convey these realizations to our kids. But when it becomes something that feels like everything else will fall into place if you do these things first or achieve X, we are not helping our kids with the emotional or interpersonal side of life. We’re creating a one-dimensional kind of person.

Sometimes parents also think that if they don’t give their child severe consequences or punishments, the child won’t learn and mature. When you try to convey information through punishment, you actually teach a child to defer to other people’s anger and control. Of course, we want them to be aware of consequences, but sometimes we can go too far. You can’t have a full, right life if you’re always anticipating that somebody might be mad at you.

Juli Fraga, Psy.D., is an AEDP-trained psychologist in San Francisco. She supports parents with kids of all ages. She is also the co-author of the new book, Parents Have Feelings, Too.

#9385. Parthenon’s east pediment, ‘the most famous image of antiquity’, recreated in Frankfurt exhibition

Marble marvels: the Liebieghaus team deduced that the sculpted group on the Parthenon’s east pediment featured the two Dioscuri horsemen seen on this Roman sarcophagus lid at the Galleria Borghese Photo: © Galleria Borghese

Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.

In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.

“Nothing came of that,” says Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.

But now, Brinkmann says his team has solved a riddle akin to “putting together a jigsaw puzzle without having all the pieces”. The results of decades of research will go on show in an exhibition, Athena, the Stage is Yours: the Parthenon Puzzle, opening at the Liebieghaus on 18 November.

Long a flashpoint in Greek-British relations, the politics of the Parthenon surfaced in the run-up to the opening. The exhibition was to include marble fragments from both the British Museum in London and the Acropolis Museum in Athens. But, as The Art Newspaper reported last month, the Greek government withdrew its loan of nine fragments: according to Greek media reports, the request was rejected by Greece’s Central Archaeological Council on the grounds that they would be shown alongside British Museum pieces removed from the Acropolis by Lord Elgin. The Greek ministry of culture’s press office did not respond to emailed requests for comment and confirmation.

Greece has for decades demanded the return of the Parthenon Marbles taken by Elgin, which have been housed in the British Museum since 1817. The Liebieghaus has, however, secured a rare loan of two fragments from the British Museum. After the Greek government’s withdrawal, a British Museum spokesperson confirmed that the museum “will still be loaning”.

“The cancellation of the loans from Greece does not detract from the exhibition’s concept, or its scholarly significance,” declares Elisabeth Pallentin, a spokesperson for the Liebieghaus. “The exhibition is based primarily on new findings resulting from many years of research at the Liebieghaus.”

The east pediment is probably “the most famous image of antiquity”, Brinkmann says, with the centre of the sculpted ensemble composed of 3.5m-tall figures. The pediment was destroyed at some point between the fifth century AD and 1670—it is not known when or why, though there are plenty of theories—and 80% of it is still missing.

The rest is in fragments in museums around the world. Until now, no one had succeeded in fully reconstructing the central figures, Brinkmann says. “In the last 200 years, there have been a lot of proposals, but we saw that there were always gaps.”

A reconstruction of the figures in the east pediment of the Parthenon (detail)

Vinzenz Brinkmann and Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, 2026. Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung, Frankfurt am Main

The most serious work on the east pediment had been undertaken more than a century ago by a British Museum curator, Arthur Hamilton Smith, Brinkmann says. Smith partially recreated the east pediment using plaster casts from the British Museum and cooperated with colleagues in Athens to obtain more casts; his reconstruction went on display in the museum in 1908.

“He did a fantastic job in preparing the way,” Brinkmann says. “That was our basis.”

Although the Liebieghaus team recreated these fragments using scans and a 3D printer, the majority of the pediment was still missing. A breakthrough came when the team began investigating reliefs from the lids of Roman sarcophagi, which proved the key to unlocking the mystery.

“It was really a chance discovery,” Brinkmann says. “During a visit to the Hermitage in St Petersburg in 2014, we noticed a figural relief on the lid of a sarcophagus that was clearly closely related to the composition of the east pediment. It refers to the few surviving figures from the corners of the pediment, such as Helios and Selene with their chariots, but also to figures that have repeatedly been proposed as having belonged to the east pediment, such as the Horae/Moirai.”

They discovered nine sarcophagi in total with relevant reliefs. Most were in the Vatican Museums and elsewhere in Rome. “They had been overlooked,” Brinkmann says. “But the Romans copied everything the Greeks did.”

Jaques Carrey, drawing of the east pediment (left-hand side), Temple of Minerva, Athens (1674)

Bibliothèque nationale de France, ref.: FOL-FC-3

None of these reliefs showed the entire east pediment ensemble; each depicted a different subset of the 39 figures. But with the aid of computer technology, the team established that the remaining fragments of the east pediment and the depictions on the reliefs were a 100% match.

The team’s research has yielded some surprises. It was not previously known, for instance, that the Dioscuri, the twin horsemen known as Castor and Pollux to the Romans, were portrayed on the pediment. The figures served as models for the giant figures on the Quirinale in Rome, which are almost identical and date from antiquity, Brinkmann says. The twins are portrayed standing next to their bucking horses with anxious expressions, straining at the reins in an effort to control them.

This portrayal of the Dioscuri makes sense only in the context of the birth of the goddess, Brinkmann says. In mythology, Athena burst forth from her father Zeus’s forehead after he had swallowed her mother. Her birth is described in the Homeric hymns as causing Mount Olympus to shake, the earth to shriek, and the sea to swell and rage.

“The Dioscuri are heroic horsemen in mythology,” Brinkmann says. “They don’t lose control of their horses. But the birth of Athena was a primordial cosmic event that unleashed a natural disaster. What we see are the consequences.” Other figures in the recreated ensemble are also responding to the cataclysm: Hermes, for instance, is depicted holding onto his hat.

Brinkmann is known internationally for his research into polychromy in ancient Greek and Roman sculpture. An exhibition he curated, Gods in Color—Painted Sculpture of Classical Antiquity, has travelled the world, having been shown in several US locations, Athens, Oxford, Istanbul, the Vatican Museums and elsewhere.

It is possible that the new Liebieghaus exhibition will travel too, Brinkmann says. But not, it seems, with marbles from the Athens collections, with recent developments giving little room to hope that a lasting settlement between Greece and the British Museum is on the horizon.

• Athena, the Stage is Yours, Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection, Frankfurt, 18 November-25 July 2027
